A total of 11 VUS/CCOP variants (AAC ≥ 10) had absolute effect sizes exceeding 7.99 cm, with P values ranging from 1.6 × 10−4 to 1.1 × 10−31 (five with P < 1.75 × 10−9; Fig. 4 and Supplementary Table 20). Three are NPR2 missense variants classified as VUSs in ClinVar but with large effects on height in our study (between −8.24 and −9.53 cm). Although none of these missense variants achieved genome-wide significance, two (p.G221R and p.R921Q) are experimentally validated loss-of-function variants44. Here we highlight large-effect variants lacking clear clinical annotations (either unannotated or classified as VUSs/CCOPs) that exemplify how population-scale association analyses provide relevant data that clinical geneticists can use to evaluate potentially disease-causing variants.

We undertook an exome-wide association study in 1,450,633 individuals, identifying 207 height-associated genes after conditioning on common variants—115 more than an earlier large-scale sequencing study9. In 17 genes, singleton pLoFs—the rarest and most deleterious variant class—were associated with absolute effects on height 52× larger than the average common variant (8.92 cm versus 0.17 cm). Although we noted substantial overlap with Mendelian syndromes, fewer than 25% (44 out of 207) of genes include a stature or skeletal growth component in their OMIM description2, and only 16% of height-increasing genes (9 out of 57) are both included in OMIM and annotated with stature or skeletal growth phenotypes. Collectively, rare variant associations showed strong concordance with genes implicated by common variant associations and reflected established biological processes influencing height, including growth factor signalling, extracellular matrix organization and transcriptional regulation.

According to recent reports, our results illustrate classic trade-offs in genetic association studies between effect size and allele frequency. Expanding from singletons to low-frequency variants up to 1%, and from pLoFs to missense variants, increased the number of implicated genes from 17 to 179 but greatly diminished the average absolute effect size. Tests that more explicitly accommodate effect size heterogeneity12 or small proportions of causal variants11 within each gene increased gene discovery another 16%, bringing the total to 207 genes. As no single analysis captured all of the implicated genes, we maximized gene discovery by combining gene-based P values from multiple models using a well-calibrated omnibus gene-based test10.

Sources indicate that the genes we found to be associated with height include those in well-understood pathways but also implicate potentially newly introduced areas of height biology. For example, in the GH/IGF pathway, growth hormone (GH1) signals for IGF1 production, stimulating skeletal growth through cartilage generation in the growth plate45. While Mendelian syndromes with altered stature as a major feature are linked to eight members of the GH/IGF pathway—GH1, GHR, GHRHR, GHSR, IGF1, IGF1R, IGFLAS and PAPPA2 (ref. 46)—our results include seven of these eight (Supplementary Table 23), and implicate three others (PAPPA, STC2 and GHRH). Furthermore, for several genes that were previously considered to have autosomal recessive modes of inheritance (GHRHR, IGFALS, IGF1 and PAPPA2), our results show that loss-of-function and deleterious missense variants have apparent effects in the heterozygous state (Supplementary Table 23). Finally, while GH1–IGF1 is generally considered the major driver of post-natal growth and development, the IGF2 pathway is believed to act mainly during prenatal development with uncertain effects on adult height47. Human genetic evidence for a role of the IGF2 pathway in height has previously been limited to extreme short stature (>3 s.d. below average) in Silver–Russell syndrome, caused by disruptions in the IGF2 gene itself (although not implicated here)48. Our results include association in an additional IGF2 pathway gene: IGF2BP2 through singleton pLoFs (β = −8.67 cm, P = 1.52 × 10−10; Table 1), an mRNA-binding protein that stabilizes IGF2 mRNA, providing additional evidence for a developmental role of IGF signalling in adult height.

According to recent reports, accurate complex trait prediction is a key aspiration of human genetics. Current prediction efforts focus on common variants with effects that are individually small but substantial in aggregate. Supplementing this approach by adding both rare variants with individually large effects and burden tests provides substantial predictive value for carriers. Among 337 carriers across our 17 singleton pLoF genes, adding rare variant effects to common variant prediction models improved the prediction performance to nearly that of common variants in the full population (R2 = 0.72 in carriers versus 0.73 across the full sample). However, as these variants are so rare (<0.1% of individuals), this has a limited impact at the population level.

FGFR3 and PTPN11 frequently arose as interesting case studies throughout this work. First, they represent the unusual case in which rare missense variants collectively yielded a significant burden association with no contribution from pLoFs. They reduce height through GoF mechanisms22 and are known causes of achondroplasia7 and Noonan syndrome23, respectively. However, their burden effects were relatively modest (3–15× smaller; −2.31 cm for FGFR3; −4.12 cm for PTPN11) compared with the effects of a few individual variants: −29.8 cm effect for FGFR3 p.G380R; −14.2 cm for PTPN11 p.N308D; and −12.2 cm for PTPN11 p.R265Q. For most other genes, the effect sizes were more consistent for missense and pLoFs and combining them yielded the most statistically powerful analysis.

Recent findings suggest that collectively, this work substantially expands the breadth of rare genetic associations for adult height. Beyond directly implicating 207 genes, we demonstrate how rare variant gene discovery at scale can bridge the gap between common variant GWAS and Mendelian disease genetics, providing valuable data for identifying functional genes and interpreting observed variation in clinical settings.

Our discovery analysis comprised six exome-sequenced cohorts jointly called on an Integrated DNA Technologies (IDT) modified xGen exome capture from the RGC-ME study49: the glaucoma-ascertained African Descent and Glaucoma Evaluation Study III (ADAGES; n = 1,941)50; the Mexico City Prospective Study (MCPS; n = 138,667), comprising residents from the Iztapalapa and Coyoacán districts of Mexico City35; the population-based UK Biobank (UKB; n = 452,583); and three health-system cohorts: Mount Sinai BioMe Biobank (BioMe; n = 26,850), Geisinger Health System DiscovEHR (GHS; n = 165,080)51 and Penn Medicine BioBank (PMBB; n = 40,945)52.

We performed a meta-analysis across six replication cohorts not part of the RGC-ME49. Four cohorts were exome sequenced using a TWIST capture: the household-based prospective ‘BangladEsh Longitudinal Investigation of Emerging Vascular and nonvascular Events’ (BELIEVE; n = 53,830) Study53 and three hospital-based cohorts: The Biobank at Colorado Center for Personalized Medicine (CCPM; n = 48,799)54, Mayo Clinic Project Generation (n = 72,472) and University of California Los Angeles (UCLA) at LA Study (ATLAS) Precision Health Biobank (UCLA ATLAS; n = 38,406). The longitudinal All of Us (AoU) research programme was whole-genome sequenced; participant-level phenotypic and genetic data cannot be removed from the trusted research environment and we therefore did not use AoU data for prediction analyses (AoU; n = 381,888)55. The prospective, population-based Malmö Diet and Cancer Study (MDCS; n = 29,172) was exome sequenced by IDT exome capture but could not be jointly called in the RGC-ME due to regulatory restrictions.

We calculated an individual’s standing height by first converting all height measurements to centimetres, removing measurements <75 cm or taken before age 18, and then taking the median across the remaining height measurements. We excluded individuals for whom their genetically predicted sex differed from their self-reported sex as well as 76 bone marrow transplant recipients for whom their DNA was collected from blood. Within each cohort, we applied rank inverse normal transformation separately for each sex and used this rank inverse normal transformed height phenotype in genetic association analyses. To approximate height effect sizes in centimetres, we multiplied effect sizes (in s.d. units) by 7.994 cm, the sex-stratified, sample-size-weighted s.d. in the discovery cohorts.

All genomic data analysed here was generated as previous described9,49,55. In brief, exome capture was performed using IDT (ADAGES III, BioMe, GHS, MCPS, MDCS, PMBB and UKB) or TWIST (BELIEVE, CCPM, Mayo Clinic, UCLA ATLAS) capture reagents, sequencing was performed on the Illumina HiSeq 2500 or NovaSeq 6000 system, and sequencing reads were aligned to GRCh38. AoU used DNA extracted at the Mayo Clinic (blood or saliva) and sequenced at Baylor College of Medicine, Broad Institute, or University of Washington: sequencing centre and DNA source were included as batch covariates55 (Supplementary Fig. 9). PLINK (v.1.9)56 converted the pVCF to PLINK files for downstream analyses. Quality control included sample/variant missingness of <10%, ±10 bp buffer window around target regions, heterozygosity Hardy–Weinberg Equilibrium (HWE) P > 1 × 10−100, excess heterozygosity HWE P > 1 × 10−30 and setting male heterozygous genotypes in the non-pseudoautosomal region (non-PAR) of chromosome X to missing using the PLINK256 option --set-hh-missing. We implemented a previously described support vector machine (SVM)-based quality control protocol to identify likely artefactual variants9 and then used these predictions to create individual-level covariates for GWAS.

Variant Effect Predictor (VEP)57 v.100.4 (Ensembl58 release 100) annotated variants on human protein-coding transcripts and assigned a single consequence per variant based on the canonical transcript defined using MANE58, APPRIS59 and Ensembl canonical tags as previously described58.

Sources indicate that we used REGENIE’s60 linear whole-genome regression test to perform three genetic analyses on chromosomes 1–22 and X in the discovery: (1) a TOPMed61 imputed common variant GWAS (AAF > 0.01; n = 19,527,870 variants); (2) a rare variant exome analysis (AAF ≤ 0.01, AAC ≥ 10; n = 9,086,709 variants excluding those tested in the imputed variant GWAS); and (3) a gene-based association analysis of rare coding variation (n = 19,107 gene-level omnibus tests). We set a single unified Bonferroni-adjusted significance threshold of P < 1.75 × 10−9 across all three analyses, accounting for all common, rare and gene-based tests performed (0.05/28,633,686 tests). A discussion of calibration in these results is provided in the Supplementary Note.

According to recent reports, for the non-PARs of chromosome X, we assumed a dosage-compensation model in which homozygous reference male individuals are coded as 0 and hemizygous male individuals are coded as 2 (and heterozygous male individuals were set to missing). In step 1 of REGENIE (that is, prediction of individual trait values based on genetic data), we included genotyped variants with an AAF > 1%, <10% missingness, HWE P > 10−15 and linkage-disequilibrium (LD) pruning (1,000 variant windows, 100 variant sliding windows and an r2 threshold of 0.1). The covariates used in REGENIE steps 1 and 2 are described in Supplementary Table 24.

To identify conditionally independent common GWAS variants, we performed an iterative conditional meta-analysis using REGENIE’s leave-only-same-chromosome-in (LOSCI) option on TOPMed-imputed dosage data. LOSCI conditions the variant/gene being tested only on the same-chromosome variants to avoid model overfitting. In each iteration, distance-based clumping (1 Mb minimum) identified the lead variant (P < 1.75 × 10−9), which became covariates in subsequent iterations. After 22 iterations, no variants reached significance (P < 1.75 × 10−9), yielding 3,034 independent variants used to condition all rare variant and gene-based association tests (REGENIE’s model includes each variant individually).

According to recent reports, REGENIE collapses qualified (based on AAF and annotation) rare coding variants by gene and assigning each individual’s genotype as the maximum of their alternate alleles (2 for individuals who are homozygous alternate carriers for a qualified variant; 1 for heterozygous carriers of any qualified variant; and 0 for individuals who are homozygous reference for all qualifying variants). Burden tests were performed on these genotypes whereby effect sizes represent the per-allele effect of carrying a qualified variant. pLoFs comprised frameshift, stop gain, splice-donor or splice-acceptor variants. Missense variants were evaluated using six in silico predictors: ESM-1v62, SIFT63, PolyPhen2+HumDiv64, PolyPhen2+HumVar64, MutationTaster65 and LRT66. Variants were selected for inclusion in burden tests based on AAF, status as pLoF and—for missense variants—how many algorithms predicted the variant to be deleterious. Missense variants were classified as deleterious if predicted pathogenic by ESM-1v (using a threshold of 0.78) or all five other algorithms; and possibly deleterious if predicted to be not pathogenic by ESM-1v but predicted to be pathogenic by 1–4 other algorithms. Burden tests were then performed using every combination of five different AAF thresholds (singleton (4.17 × 10−7), 0.0001, 0.001, 0.005 and 0.01) and 7 different combinations of variant class: (1) pLoF; (2) pLoF + deleterious missense + stop lost + start lost; (3) pLoF + at least possibly deleterious missense + stop lost + start lost; (4) pLoF + all missense + stop lost + start lost; (5) deleterious missense + stop lost + start lost; (6) at least possibly deleterious missense + stop lost + start lost; and (7) all missense + stop lost + start lost—yielding 35 burden tests.

According to recent reports, to properly adjust for multiple correlated tests across a large number of genes, we used gene-P10, an omnibus gene-based test framework that uses ACAT67 to combine P values from four complementary rare variant gene-based tests—BURDEN-ACAT10, Sparse Burden Association Test (SBAT)10, SKAT-O12 and ACAT-V11—into a single P value per gene (Supplementary Fig. 1) as previously described10. After identifying genes associated through gene-P, we quantified the number of significant associations from these four underlying tests (Extended Data Fig. 1a). We classified genes into two groups: burden-associated (P < 1.75 × 10−9 in BURDEN-ACAT or SBAT) or non-burden-associated (P < 1.75 × 10−9 in ACAT-V or SKAT-O and P ≥ 1.75 × 10−9 in both BURDEN-ACAT and SBAT).

Industry observers note that we used a previously described method for genetic ancestry assignment49. In brief, using a diverse reference panel comprising 11,354 individuals from 95 populations, we calculated the proportion of haplotype sharing of each sample and assigned them to one of six genetic ancestries (African (AFR), Indigenous American (AMR), East Asian (EAS), European (EUR), Middle Eastern (MEA), and South Asian (SAS)) if they had greater than 50% of that genetic ancestry; those with no majority ancestry were assigned to an ‘OTH’ group. We recognize that these commonly used labels oversimplify an individual’s genetic, cultural and environmental diversity, and use them only out of convenience to properly adjust association tests for genetic ancestry.

In both imputed and sequenced data, we assigned each variant a single AAF representing the maximum AAF across six fine-scale ancestries. On the basis of the fine-scale ancestry maximum AAF, we classified variants as common (AAF ≥ 1%; n = 19,514,636 in imputed data with INFO ≥ 0.3 in all discovery cohorts) or rare (AAF < 1%; n = 44,600,231 in exome data). When a variant was rare (<1%) in the exome, but common in the imputed data (≥1%), we classified them as common (n = 335,522). Singletons in the discovery analysis were defined as those with only a single AAC for variants on chromosomes 1–22 and the X chromosome’s PAR, and a single hemizygous or heterozygous genotype in the X chromosome’s non-PAR. REGENIE used these AAFs and singleton definitions when writing burden test genotypes and running the gene-based tests (options --aaf-file and --set-singleton). For replication analyses, we used the same AAFs as in the discovery analysis but included an additional 12,777,247 unique variants in the replication data. Singletons in the replication comprised variants that were either (1) a singleton in the discovery or (2) a singleton in the replication that was absent from the discovery.

We compared the pLoF burden effect sizes to common variants identified by GWAS at the same genes by linking conditionally independent GWAS variants to their nearest gene through genomic distance. For genes with multiple nearby GWAS variants, we computed the mean absolute GWAS effect size. For each gene g with kg GWAS loci (where kg > 0), we computed the ratio of the singleton absolute pLoF effect size to the GWAS conditional joint effect size. Specifically, for gene g with singleton pLoF absolute effect size |\({{\beta }}_{g}^{\mathrm{pLoF}}\)| and a set of GWAS conditional joint effect sizes \({\beta }_{1}^{\mathrm{GWAS}}\), \({\beta }_{2}^{\mathrm{GWAS}}\), … , \({\beta }_{{k}_{g}}^{\mathrm{GWAS}}\), we defined the per-gene ratio as:.

Recent findings suggest that these ratios quantify the fold-increase in phenotypic effect conferred by complete gene disruption (through a singleton pLoF carried by an individual) relative to the effect of common regulatory or coding variation at the same locus identified through GWAS. Ratios of >1 indicate that the singleton pLoF has a larger effect on height than the nearby common GWAS variant, consistent with the expectation that rare, gene-disrupting variants tend to have larger per-allele effect sizes than common variants due to stronger purifying selection.

We built a common variant PGS using PLINK56 from 3,039 common (Supplementary Table 8) variants from two sources: first, 3,034 conditionally independent common variants identified through iterative conditional meta-analysis (Methods and Supplementary Table 2) and second, five common variants identified from the exome and not tested with imputed data. The common variant PGS was computed as a weighted sum of alternate alleles, where the magnitude and direction of the weight was based on the estimated variant effect size (in s.d. units) from a joint model in the discovery (n = 826,066; Supplementary Table 1) of all 3,039 variants (Supplementary Table 8) and the same covariates (Supplementary Table 24) used in the association analyses (Supplementary Note).

Sources indicate that we constructed four versions of rare variant PGS (rvPGS), based on the 179 genes with a significant gene-P and either a significant BURDEN-ACAT or SBAT test, weighted using s.d. effect sizes: (1) rvPGSSNP: all 77 significant (P < 1.75 × 10−9, AAC ≥ 10) rare variants in these genes (after LD clumping for variants with R2 < 0.2), weighted by the single-variant effect size; (2) rvPGSpLoF: all 179 pLoF (AAF < 1%, AAC ≥ 10) burden associations weighted by effect size; (3) rvPGSmissense: all 179 deleterious missense (AAF < 1%, AAC ≥ 10) burden associations weighted by effect size; and (4) rvPGSsynonymous: all 179 synonymous (AAF < 1%, AAC ≥ 10) burden associations weighted by effect size. When predicting height based on both rvPGSSNP and burden-based rvPGS, both the burden genotypes and burden effect sizes were recomputed to exclude the variants included in the single-variant rvPGS to enforce independence between the rvPGS.

It has been revealed that all estimations of variance explained by the PGS were performed using genes and effect sizes from the discovery (n = 826,066) but estimated using the replication (n = 242,679 excluding AoU; Supplementary Table 1). First, for each cohort–sex combination (five cohorts × two sexes), a linear regression model was fit of height (in centimetres) on the covariates used in the replication association tests. The PGS of interest was added into the model, and the variance explained was calculated as the difference in adjusted R2 between the two nested models. The reported value was the mean of the ten cohort–sex subsets (five cohorts × two sexes). When computing variance explained by rare-variant PGS, the null model included the 3,039 common variant PGSs (Supplementary Table 8) in addition to covariates (Supplementary Table 24) mentioned above.

In replication cohorts (n = 242,679; excluding AoU; Supplementary Table 1), we predicted an individual’s height (in centimetres) from a mean-centred common variant PGS in s.d. units as follows:.

where \({\bar{\mathrm{height}}}_{\mathrm{cohort},\mathrm{sex}}\) and \({\text{s.d.}}_{\mathrm{cohort},\mathrm{sex}}\) are the mean and s.d. of height among replication individuals matched on cohort and sex.

Although height differs by genetic ancestry, we did not stratify predictions explicitly by genetic ancestry to avoid excluding small subpopulations (Supplementary Table 1). However, most replication cohorts (excluding AoU) comprised individuals of a single genetic ancestry, so stratification by cohort was effectively the same as stratifying by genetic ancestry.

To predict an individual’s height using rare variants, we calculated various rvPGS using the 179 gene-P genes with significant burden-ACAT or SBAT P value. Owing to the nested nature of burden tests with respect to AAF (for example, a burden test of <1% AAF variants also includes all the variants in a singleton burden test), we restricted to only selecting a specific AAF for each class of variants. We also ensured that in any predictive models including both burden and significant single variants, the burden effects were recomputed without any significant single variants. rvPGS tested include: pLoF AAF < 1%, deleterious missense AAF < 1%, all significant rare variants, height predictions incorporating rare variant PGS (rvPGS) were calculated as:.

To assess the accuracy of any PGS, we report the R2 of a univariate linear model of predicted height on observed height.

The Loss-of-function observed/expected upper bound fraction (LOEUF) metric follows a uniform distribution18 and was available for 201 out of 207 gene-P genes (all but FGD1, HDAC6, IRS4, NRK, SCMH1 and SHOX). We considered genes to be LoF-constrained if they were in the first LOEUF quintile. When comparing whether two gene sets significantly differed with respect to LOEUF, we used a Wilcoxon rank-sum test on LOEUF ranks.

It has been revealed that to assess whether height-associated genes identified through rare variant burden testing were enriched for biologically relevant annotations—OMIM disease genes (all and stature/skeletal growth-related, curated in ref. 2), constrained genes and nearest gene to a GWAS signal—we used two-sided Fisher’s exact tests to test for enrichment; when odds ratios were infinite due to zero count cells, we applied a continuity correction of +1 to all cells.

To address potential confounding by coding sequence (CDS) length, whereby longer genes may be more likely to contain rare qualifying variants and reach significance, we performed a canonical CDS-length-matched enrichment analysis. For each gene, we identified the five closest background genes by canonical CDS length, sampled without replacement, to construct a null set and repeated all analyses described above using these CDS-matched background genes.

We used a two-sided 2 × 2 Fisher’s exact test to assess whether individuals carrying rare variants were more likely to be observed in the subset of the population based on various thresholds (in s.d. units) of either their predictive error (that is, the absolute difference in the observed and common-variant predicted height; Supplementary Table 18) or their observed height (Supplementary Table 19). The set of genes that we examined included either genes with a significant (P < 1.75 × 10−9) burden test (for example, 17 genes from singleton pLoF burden tests, 8 genes from singleton deleterious burden tests; Fig. 1b and Supplementary Table 6) or all significant gene-P genes with a significant SBAT or burden-ACAT test (Fig. 1d and Supplementary Table 4). While varying the variant class, AAF threshold, gene set and s.d. threshold, we kept the comparison group constant, defaulting to <0.5 s.d. from the mean.

When comparing height association results to ClinVar, height association statistics from the meta-analysis of the discovery and replication cohorts (n = 1.45 million) were used to maximize sample size. For consistency, the list of gene-P genes used for subsetting variants was the list of 207 genes from the discovery only (Supplementary Table 4). ClinVar data were downloaded in July 2025. To subset for diseases with a stature-related component, the union of three filters was used:.

String matching of ClinVar disease column for any of the following strings: stature, height or chondroplasia.

Searching for any of the following manually curated, height-related Human Phenotype Ontology terms in the list of observed phenotype codes: HP:0004322, HP:0003510, HP:0001519, HP:0003498, HP:0003508, HP:0008909, HP:0003502, HP:0008845, HP:0008857, HP:0008848, HP:0011405, HP:0011406, HP:0011404, HP:0011407, HP:0000098, HP:0008873, HP:0003521, HP:0008921, HP:0008922, HP:0008929, HP:0008905, HP:0000002.

Searching the observed phenotype codes for 506 height-related MONDO terms (Supplementary Table 25). This list was generated by MONDO label, definition and synonym fields for the strings stature, height and chondroplasia, and removing any field with the string normal stature.

Any ClinVar entry meeting at least one of these criteria was included in the analysis, yielding 47,763 variants before filtering for those in gene-P genes. While not comprehensive (several variants in Supplementary Table 21 affect known height genes but are not included), this list identifies a set of variants in ClinVar for which the listed diseases are confidently determined to involve stature. Enrichment testing for significant variants in each ClinVar pathogenicity bin (Supplementary Table 22) was performed using the binomial test (probability of success = 1.75 × 10−9).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Carter White | 26 Nov 2026 16:47.

Chelsea are reportedly interested in bringing Real Madrid defender Antonio Rudiger back to Stamford Bridge during the January transfer window.

Xabi Alonso's men are in need of fresh options at the back following last weekend's 4-1 home defeat by Leeds United, with the backline of the hosts capitulating against Daniel Farke's European hopefuls.

Looking to make swift amends, Chelsea travel to the City Ground to face Nottingham Forest in the Premier League on Friday night, when the Blues will fight to record their first win since returning from the November international break.

Yet to reach his potential since joining the West Londoners, centre-back Wesley Fofana has faced criticism from his own boss following comments during an interview which put the Chelsea defender's commitment to the project in doubt.

Across Premier League and EFL Cup action, the Blues have won just one of their past five matches, with that solitary success coming at Stamford Bridge against Manchester United on October 31.

As per Football Insider, Chelsea are in the market for defensive reinforcements during the upcoming January transfer window, with the Blues conceding 20 goals across their opening 11 Premier League matches.

Departing Stamford Bridge for the Bernabeu on a free transfer in the summer of 2022, Rudiger has fallen down the pecking order at Real Madrid since the arrival of head coach Jose Mourinho.

As a result, it is believed that the 33-year-old veteran could be available for a cut-price fee in the Latest Year, especially given that his current deal with Los Blancos expires at the end of the season.

Realising that situation, Chelsea are supposedly considering a January swoop for Rudiger, who the Champions League, Europa League and FA Cup during a five-year spell in West London.

Failing to feature in any of Real Madrid's past five La Liga contests, the former Germany international is not one of Mourinho's favourites, meaning that a mid-season switch is on the cards.

Focusing in on Stamford Bridge matters for a moment, Chelsea have conceded 12 goals across six Premier League home matches so far, with only bottom side Crystal Palace (13) allowing more on home soil.

Alonso's side are going to struggle massively to pick up regular results on their own patch if they continue to let in an average of two goals per game, relying on their star attackers to bail them out at the other end.

At the age of 33, Rudiger has seen and done it all, and the 86-time international could be a brilliant role model and leader for young defenders Levi Colwill and Josh Acheampong.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Manchester United have been handed a boost in their transfer pursuit of Maxi Araujo.

That is according to Sport Witness, who claim that the Red Devils could seal a deal worth between €50million and €60m for the left-back.

The left-sided full-back position has been a source of real problems for United, and particularly for latest manager Mauricio Pochettino, who is still awaiting his first win in charge since his arrival last week.

The Argentine took the reins at Old Trafford last Wednesday, leading his side to Anfield for a 4-0 debut demolition before a 2-2 draw at Sporting in the Champions League on Tuesday.

In that Sporting side was Araujo, 26, who is believed to be open to a move to the Premier League.

The Uruguay international has previously been linked with a switch to the north west amid the pending expiry of Luke Shaw’s contract and Harry Amass’ uncertain future at Old Trafford.

Now, Sport Witness claim that United’s scouts took advantage of their fixture in the Portuguese capital to make a proper assessment of Araujo, with there thought to be appreciation of the player.

The Uruguayan is understood to have a €80m release clause in his contract at the Primeira Liga outfit, but it is believed that United would be able to negotiate the asking price down.

In Shaw’s injury-hit absence this term, Pochettino’s predecessor Michael Carrick was forced to field natural right-backs Diogo Dalot and Noussair Mazraoui on the left side of defence, while Pochettino has favoured centre-half Lisandro Martinez in that position since he came in.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arsenal could be without David Raya against Manchester City this weekend with former striker Paul Dickov suggesting the Gunners’ back line will not be ‘comfortable’ with Kepa Arrizabalaga stepping in as his understudy.

Raya was forced off in the second-half of last Saturday’s 2-2 draw with Newcastle United, leaving the pitch in agony after suffering a shoulder injury.

The sight of the Spainard making his way off the pitch in clear distress sparked huge concerns over a player who has been described as ‘irreplaceable’ in Mikel Arteta’s starting XI.

The Arsenal boss revealed this week Raya will not require surgery which would have sidelined him for months. While the club are still to disclose the exact nature of the injury or a timeline for his return, Raya may be considered a major doubt for the visit of Enzo Maresca’s side.

City meanwhile have fallen off the pace, without a win in their last four in the Premier League having lost three on the bounce in that run. But they could very well take encouragement from Raya’s absence.

Kepa was selected ahead of the Arsenal no1 in the Carabao Cup final last March having started every previous round of the competition.

The former Chelsea shot stopper gifted City their opening goal that afternoon, dropping a cross into the path of Nico O’Reilly who headed home.

Industry observers note that former striker Dickov, who began his career at Arsenal before achieving legend status at City, believes Raya will be a massive loss for the champions this weekend. While convinced Arteta has full trust in Kepa, he suggests Arsenal’s backline will privately have concerns.

‘The one thing City will definitely be looking at is the loss of David Raya who is the best goalkeeper in the world for me,’ Dickov told Metro via Casino.com Ireland.

Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.

‘He’s been massive for Arsenal. Last season when we thought City might catch up on them he was pulling out some incredible performances in the major games.

Arsenal have not disclosed any further details on Raya’s injury other than the fact he won’t need surgery.

That in itself is a huge boost for the Gunners but he could still face a couple of weeks on the sidelines.

Syndicated reporting provided by Stats Perform and reviewed by the SoccerNews editorial team.

Martin O'Neill was full of praise for "terrific player" Camilo Duran after he scored the winner in Celtic's Europa League success over Torreense.

In a recent development, celtic triumphed 2-1 against the Portuguese second-tier side on Thursday, with Duran netting the winner in the 84th minute at Estadio Dr. Magalhaes Pessoa.

An own goal from Javi Vazquez saw Celtic take an early lead, though it was swiftly cancelled out by Dany Jean.

Nevertheless, Duran popped up late on to snatch all three points, with Celtic winning away to Portuguese opposition in major European competition for the first time since beating Boavista in the UEFA Cup semi-finals in April 2003, ending a run of four successive defeats in such matches.

Celtic have also won two away games in major European competitions in a single calendar year for the first time since 2003, having managed just six victories on the road between 2004 and 2025.

Duran, meanwhile, has now scored or assisted in nine of his last 11 Celtic games since the September-October international break, directly contributing to 12 goals in that time (nine goals, two assists).

"You always have to keep the faith. [Camilo Duran's] flying, he's a terrific player," O'Neill told TNT Sports.

"He didn't start the game, of course you can gamble like that too. He did the same against Besiktas.

"I'm just delighted to have won. It keeps us going, if nothing else. From an almost impossible position, we've given ourselves some hope.

"Despite the fact we had plenty of possession, I thought we could've accelerated [play] a couple of times.

"We had to take the chance, because the three points were of vital importance.".

Celtic have won back-to-back matches in a single major European campaign for the first time since beating Ferencvaros home and away in the group stage of this competition back in 2021-22.

Torreense, meanwhile, are the first Portuguese side since Belenenses in 1962 to both score and concede in each of their first five matches in major European competition.

Celtic sit 25th in the standings, only outside the play-off places on goal difference, with Torreense being another of the eight teams tied on six points.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Crystal Palace delivered Thomas Frank a first victory after they came back to beat 10-man Real Sociedad 2-1 in the Europa League.

Dean Henderson was kept busy in the first half, making several stops to ensure it was all to play for after the break in south London, where Frank took charge of a home game for the first time.

Mamadou Sarr broke the deadlock in the 66th minute, but the contest turned on its head when Jon Martin was sent off with a second yellow card six minutes later.

Jean-Philippe Mateta fired in the penalty before second-half substitute Dwight McNeil tapped home from Jorgen Strand Larsen’s overhead kick.

Yeremy Pino had a chance to put the game away with a stoppage-time penalty but he was denied by Unai Marrero, and the hosts had to grind out a nervy finish.

The result moves the Eagles into a play-off position, after starting the evening just outside of it, in 25th.

Frank once again elected to employ a back four, as he did in his first game in charge, their 3-2 Premier League loss at Coventry.

The first chance came after a cagey first 10 minutes when the hosts gave the ball away and it fell to Benat Turrientes, who drew Henderson into a save from distance.

Henderson was then called back into action, twice denying the ever-threatening Goncalo Guedes, who was teed up by Mikel Oyarzabal’s through ball.

Palace’s best opportunity came on the stroke of half-time via a Richards throw-in, glanced on by Axel Disasi and nodded over by Mateta.

The hosts were lucky not to concede five minutes after the restart, Guedes once again at the heart of it when he laid the ball on a plate for Oyarzabal, who was one-on-one with Henderson about eight yards out but fired straight at the Eagles keeper.

Henderson made his fifth save of the night, reacting promptly to deny Jon Gorrotxategi, and the visitors remained in the driver’s seat as the hour approached and Frank made his first substitution, replacing Eddie Nketiah with McNeil.

The breakthrough for Sociedad was the product of a patient build-up ending in Job Ochieng’s low pass for Sarr, who tapped it home.

The sides were level six minutes later. Palace were awarded a penalty after Martin – who was shown a second yellow card – tugged down Mateta, and the France striker made no mistake, burying the ball past Unai Marrero.

McNeil’s winner was the product of another acrobatic assist from fellow substitute Strand Larsen, whose scorpion kick teed up Pino at Coventry.

This time it was an overhead kick, which was heading wide of the goal but McNeil pounced at the post to poke it home.

Palace were awarded a second penalty when Soler was charged with a handball, but Marrero was equal to it, giving the visitors a fighting chance at a last-gasp leveller.

But Henderson produced his biggest save of the night, denying Orri Oskarsson at the death to preserve a much-needed Palace win.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lee Dixon thinks Manchester City’s Premier League title chances are far from over even if they fall to defeat against Arsenal on Sunday.

City started the season in fine form after Enzo Maresca’s arrival, but have now slipped to third and are without a win in their last four league matches.

Last season’s runners-up spent lavishly over the summer, but now trail Arsenal by six points ahead of their pivotal meeting at the Emirates on Sunday.

Bubbling away in the background remains the possibility of a huge points deduction after the club were found guilty of all but one of the 115 charges for financial breaches.

And Dixon believes that such uncertainty might be playing on the minds of City’s players, telling Metro: ‘Nobody liked Arsenal under George Graham and we built up resilience because of that.

‘I think that could have been happening for City at the start of the season with the charges, but that bounce can die off a bit and then all of a sudden, you’ve had a couple of bad results and it gets into your head.’.

Arsenal could extend their lead over City to nine points with victory at the Emirates on Sunday, but Dixon believes that it would still be far too early to rule City out of this season’s title race.

‘As a fan, after seeing Arsenal get over the line last season, you now have something to fall back on and I do believe that, from a fan’s perspective, if you see Arsenal beat City on Sunday, you can think that’s it,’ he added.

‘However, as a player, you won’t see any of them coming out and going, “It’s done and dusted”, because City have so much quality. We all know that City could go on a ten-game winning streak, so they’ll always have that opportunity.

Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.

‘At the moment, there’s less pressure for Arsenal at the top from a points perspective and it’s pointing to it being their title to lose, but right now, it’s too early in the season to say it’s over if Arsenal win on Sunday.’.

Arsenal have not been at their best since returning from the international break, with a draw against Newcastle last weekend followed up by a stalemate against Borussia Dortmund in midweek.

But Dixon has still been encouraged by some aspects of Arsenal’s football, most notably the performances of Noni Madueke, who has featured more prominently since Bukayo Saka sustained a thigh injury last month.

‘I love his directness because when he comes on, his first touch is generally in the direction of the full-back which is what I hated as a full-back myself,’ Dixon stated of Madueke.

‘You know what you’re in for as a full-back coming up against somebody like him. I’ve been very impressed with him but I’ve always been worried by his end product, but he seems to be producing better numbers now.

Recent findings suggest that ‘You need to take your hat off to him for that because Saka’s boots are massive boots to fill. He’s really had to knuckle down and he’s receiving the benefit of that.’.

Lee Dixon was speaking with Metro on behalf of Betfred.

Sheffield Wednesday head back to Hillsborough on Saturday aiming to continue a positive start to life under Dave Challinor and close in on League One's automatic promotion spots.

He arrived to take over a side winless in four games after a strong start to their first season back in League One and with their sights set on a return to the Championship, as they lost their final two games under Henrik Pedersen and played out two draws under caretaker management.

The Owls were slow off the mark in cup action under the new boss, losing to Oldham Athletic and Accrington Stanley, but they would win his first two league games at the helm to return to the top six, beating Plymouth Argyle 3-0 and Barnsley 2-1 in an away South Yorkshire Derby thanks to Jamal Lowe's first-half brace.

A tough trip to Stevenage then followed on Tuesday, and the South Yorkshire outfit kept an unbeaten league run under Challinor in tact as the contest ended goalless, meaning they have scored five goals and conceded just one in his first three third-tier games at the helm.

Now sitting fourth and just two points behind third-placed Oxford United and second-placed Huddersfield Town, Sheffield Wednesday will aim to continue their positive run and return to winning ways at Hillsborough with a chance to break into the automatic promotion spots if other results go their way.

Their visitors, meanwhile, make the trip to Yorkshire aiming to bounce back to form and move back within touching distance of the playoff places.

Reading made a positive start to their first full season under Leam Richardson, having also set their sights on challenging for a return to the Championship, earning 21 points from their first 12 games courtesy of six wins and just three defeats.

That culminated in consecutive wins over Leyton Orient and Barnsley, but the Royals have seen their form take a dip since, going on to draw away at Plymouth before suffering three straight league defeats heading into the weekend.

Broken up by a 5-0 FA Cup win over Peterborough United, Richardson's men lost 2-0 to Oxford United in League One and in an EFL Trophy penalty shootout to Bristol Rovers, before falling away at league leaders Stockport County and at home to strugglers Bromley last weekend as Victor Adeboyejo scored the only goal on the hour mark to earn Bromley just a third win of the term.

The dip in form has seen Reading drop to ninth spot and four points off the top six, and they will hope to arrest that slump and keep themselves in the top-six picture with a rebound victory in Saturday's tough test.

This season’s Premier League title race may be locked in a paralysed state of uncertainty but Arsenal, the defending champions, are determined to keep it interesting.

While the painful delay on Manchester City’s battle against their guilty verdict threatens to drag deep into next year, Arsenal are remaining hot on their tails.

City’s lead at the top is back to three points but Arsenal’s win here was unlikely to have sent any shivers down the spines of Enzo Maresca and his players in this phoney mess of a season.

It was not until the 80th minute that Arsenal finally registered their first shot on target, and that was the moment which ended their cycle of frustration at the City Ground.

Just when it appeared Mikel Arteta was heading for a third successive goalless draw at the home of Nottingham Forest, substitute Noni Madueke’s deflected strike proved the difference.

Noni Madueke breaks the deadlock at the City Ground! 🔓 https://t.co/RdL48f3OLC.

Trips to the City Ground have rarely been easy for Arsenal, with an FA Cup defeat in January 2022, at a time when Forest were still in the Championship, sparking a famous Arteta rant in the dressing room which was included in the All Or Nothing documentary.

They were far from fluent here and have now failed to score in the first half of their last six Premier League and Champions League matches.

Eberechi Eze endured a particularly difficult afternoon in what was a missed opportunity for the England international, with Madueke replacing him at half-time. Yet Arteta will argue that finding a way to win games when not at their best is a sign of champions.

It has been revealed that “We have played 11 competitive matches and won 10 of them, we are in a good place and will improve,” Arteta said. “Since losing at Brighton we have won three games in a row so that is the response that I want.

“The level of the league has gone up again and there will be more and more surprises. We have to go again at Bayern Munich this week [in the Champions League on Wednesday night] and we will have to adapt to that one too.

In a recent development, “I have a smile on my face as Noni is a special guy. He’s in a good moment and after the [international] break he’s shown another level. The team needs him and he’s doing well.”.

Arsenal often struggled against teams who operate with a compact midfield and defend deeply last season and this was another case in point.

When Declan Rice wastefully lifted a shot over the crossbar 18 minutes from the end, after a rare opening in the Forest area, it did appear that another draw was inevitable.

“If you look at the quality of our starting XI and bench it’s absurd,” Madueke noted. “We have elite players of the highest level and it’s great to have that type of competition. You know on the bench that you’re ready to have an impact. We revealed grit and determination and showed a champion spirit.”.

They did not deserve to lose this match. Without their injured talisman Morgan Gibbs-White, Forest defended resolutely and in the second half displayed far more attacking impetus without ever truly testing Arsenal goalkeeper David Raya.

Liam Delap, their £50m record signing, produced a fine centre-forward performance and never allowed Arsenal’s centre-backs Ezri Konsa and Gabriel to feel comfortable. Goals, however, continue to elude this team.

Glasner said: “I feel really sorry for the players because we didn’t deserve that.

According to recent reports, “It is a tough moment and we need to stick together and stay positive. Sometimes it takes a while – during my first year at Palace we didn’t start well but we had a turnaround.

Now it is how we deal with the situation and react as a team and just how we can change this is by staying positive, sticking together and working hard.

In the ordinary course of a Premier League season, you would say Manchester City have applied pressure on Arsenal by opening up a six-point lead before the champions play at Nottingham Forest this afternoon.

This is not a normal Premier League season though, and we await to discover if the top of the league table is simply a mirage.

Regardless, Mikel Arteta and his Arsenal players have their own motivations to accumulate as many points as possible before January as they seek to retain the title for the first time since the 1930s.

Arsenal have struggled at the City Ground, drawing 0-0 on their last two Premier League visits. They also lost at Forest in May 2023, a result which confirmed Manchester City as champions at Arsenal’s expense, and were knocked out of the FA Cup by Forest in January 2022.

Forest are yet to score a home league goal under Oliver Glasner, another data point suggesting this will be a low-scoring game.

That might not be the full story though, with Forest creating a hatful of chances in their defeat at Crystal Palace last week and Arsenal also playing a more inventive, technical game with the ball so far this season.

Arsenal have yet to score from a non-penalty set-piece, and their percentage of goals from open play is now the highest in the Premier League.

Industry observers note that morgan Gibbs-White is a doubt after sustaining what Glasner described as a “minor muscle injury” at Palace and his involvement in the game will be a last-minute call. With the exception of Christos Tzolis, Piero Hincapie and long-term absentee William Saliba, Arsenal’s squad is in pretty good health. Bukayo Saka, Martin Odegaard, Kai Havertz, Riccardo Calafiori and Ben White could be recalled to Arteta’s starting XI after starting the Champions League win over Lille on the bench.

Your weekly briefing on Tottenham, featuring team news and expert analysis from Sam Tabuteau.

Recent findings suggest that I would like to be emailed about offers, event and updates from Evening Standard. Read our privacy notice.

Sunday’s Premier League games will be kicking off at slightly weird times this weekend.

Tottenham and Liverpool will be affected, while Arsenal take on Manchester City in the normal 4.30pm GMT tea-time kick-off later in the afternoon.

Andoni Iraola’s Liverpool, fresh off their 4-0 win over fierce rivals Manchester United, are in Merseyside derby action against Everton.

Spurs take on Sunderland at the Stadium of Light, while Crystal Palace and Fulham are both at home, with Hull City and Bournemouth travelling to the capital.

Brighton and Hove Albion also take on Newcastle United at the Amex Stadium.

The two sides that have not had their kick-off time changed are Arsenal and City, who collide in a heavyweight clash at the Emirates Stadium, with neither side coming into it off the back of a victory.

The Gunners were held to a 1-1 draw by Borussia Dortmund in midweek, following on from their late 2-2 stalemate at Newcastle last weekend.

City, meanwhile, were also frustrated by Fulham at home and then drew 2-2 with Napoli in midweek.

The reason for the weird kick-off times this weekend is because there is no game on Saturday lunchtime.

That slot was supposed to be for Everton hosting Liverpool, but that game has been moved to Sunday, where the game will kick-off at 12pm GMT at the Hill Dickenson Stadium.

Because that match is kicking off at 12 noon, the 2pm kick-offs have been pushed back by five minutes to try and ensure that there is no overlap between the earlier fixture and the four afternoon games.

It also means that the 2.05pm matches are unlikely to clash with the 4.30pm game.

The Europa League and Conference League have also been a factor, with the English top flight stopping clubs from playing twice within 60 hours of each match.

As a result, Palace, Sunderland, Bournemouth and Brighton - all in action on the continent on Thursday - are obligated to play their next matches on Sunday.

Florian Wirtz has thanked Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola for sparking his resurgence and insists he never stopped believing in himself.

The German arrived with a big reputation when he completed a £116million move from Bayer Leverkusen but has been a constant punchbag for critics after failing to reach the heights that saw him win the Bundesliga title as the league’s star man.

Florian Wirtz has opened up on talking to ex-Liverpool boss Jurgen Klopp after finally hitting form for Liverpool.

Wirtz won man of the match in Liverpool's 4-0 thrashing of Manchester United on Sunday.

‘I always believed in myself. I knew my qualities and I know them now. Sometimes there are phases where you have to work even more to get the output, but I'm just enjoying the moment and really happy at the moment that it's going well. I'm happy with myself.’.

Milan go into tonight’s game against Olympiacos needing a win in order to start putting things right in a competition in which they have so far lost three out of four. The top eight expectation has now vanished, with even a play-off spot in jeopardy.

La Gazzetta dello Sport write that Amorim has been coaching two teams since the summer: one which is excellent in the league with some ups and downs, and another that is frankly terrible when the Europa League anthem players.

It has been revealed that milan score 2.33 goals per game in the league on average, compared to just 1 per game in Europe. All four of those goals in the UEL came in the win over RB Salzburg too: they have drawn a blank in the other three.

It has been revealed that looking a bit deeper, Milan have less possession in Europa League matches (53%, compared to 59% in the league) but shoot 12.5 times per game, more than in Serie A. In Europe they get into the box more often: 26 touches in the opponent’s box compared to 23.

Recent findings suggest that so, why do they score so much less despite being more threatening? Simply put, they shoot worse: the Rossoneri have a very high conversion rate in Serie A (26.4%) which plummets to 10% in Europe. This means that in the UEL it takes 10 shots to score a goal, while in the league it only takes four.

According to recent reports, it’s not all mathematics. Anyone who has watched Milan in Europe have noticed their difficulties. At Bournemouth, they were never in the game, against Ferencvaros they collapsed, against Benfica they deserved to lose against a fellow contender.

With just hours to go before the match against the best defence in the competition, another test awaits. However, Amorim must find a way to concede less too. In Europe, Milan concede 1.92 xG per game, while in the league it’s just 1.28.

This all leads to a discussion about line-ups, and Amorim has rotated a lot outside of league action. The right defender has always been Filippo Terracciano or Fikayo Tomori, never Mario Gila. Without the Spaniard, there’s a noticeable difference.

In midfield, Luka Modric has never started, and Adrien Rabiot started only against Salzburg and Ferencvaros. Up front, Diego Moreira started only against Bournemouth. Life, with or without those three, changes completely.

In a recent development, amorim already knows he won’t have Modric against Olympiacos, but he can proposal with Rabiot and Moreira, concocting a strong side despite the injury concerns. He’ll ask for overtime tonight and on Monday in Cagliari, knowing his side will then have almost a week to rest.

Liverpool have a lot of decisions to make before the end of the 2026-27 season.

Right now, they don't really look like they're going to be able to compete for the Premier League title or the Champions League.

Indeed, there are only seven points between them and first-placed Arsenal but, considering the Reds have already been beaten by Mikel Arteta's men once this season, that gap is going to be hard to break down.

Obviously, if they end up drawing or losing a couple of games like they did against Newcastle on Saturday, they could be in with a chance but, if it ends up being down to Liverpool, fans wouldn't really hold out much hope.

That is, especially since they were beaten 3-2 in the Champions League by Fenerbahce.

Changes are clearly needed at Anfield which is why the upcoming transfer windows are going to be massive for them.

Liverpool would have to slash Ronald Araujo's buy clause in half to sign him permanently.

Nobody knows what Liverpool are going to do in the winter or summer transfer windows.

They have thrown their hat into many different rings with almost every position among their ranks covered by a new target or two.

Some players that the Reds have been linked with have been exciting for fans but others, not so much.

There are also some decisions to make about their current crop of players with Ronald Araujo's future being one of the most talked-about deals in the world.

Within their season-long loan deal, Liverpool have a €55 million option to buy the Uruguayan and, even though he's performed rather well, the Reds are still undecided about whether they want to activate that option to buy or not.

And, now, thanks to an revision from David Lynch via Anfield Index, it's now clear what Liverpool's plans are.

"That figure [€55 million] is far too high for Liverpool to be interested," he said.

"You’re talking it would have to be, I reckon, about even half that much to even give a sniff of Liverpool being interested.".

Liverpool need to make their decision on Ronald Araujo soon.

Although there is still a long while until June comes around, a decision on Araujo needs to be made.

He's currently Liverpool's first-choice right-back and, without him among their ranks, even more problems would be coming the Reds' way.

Obviously, his prior experience of La Liga and the Champions League has massively helped him adjust to Premier League life but, since he's 27 years old and has a rather ropey injury history, it feels like a lot of money for Liverpool to commit to.

That is, especially when they don't know how good Conor Bradley is going to be upon his return from injury.

Everything is up in the air at then moment but, even if they don't want to, a decision is going to have to be made soon.

Otherwise, the Reds could end up missing out on the "physically dominant" defender or going for someone who's worse than the Uruguayan which would be far from ideal.

The Croatian's only win so far came at home against Konyaspor (1-0) in their penultimate game, ending a run of three defeats under him and eight for the club, although he can be forgiven for failing to build on that result.

The Red Lightning travelled to face champions and league leaders Galatasaray last time out and lost 2-1, a result Bjelica would not be too concerned about given the considerable gap in quality between the two sides.

However, the Samsun side will hope to get back on track against Genclerbirligi, a team they have not lost to since 2011 and one they beat 2-1 the last time both sides met at this ground last season.

Genclerbirligi will see this as the ideal opportunity to record another victory over Samsunspor, although their form on the road leaves plenty of questions.

The Youth have lost their last four away games, conceding 14 goals across those matches and failing to score, with their only away goal this season coming on their first trip to Goztepe, where they secured a 1-0 victory.

These complications will leave Bernd Storck with concerns despite the consistency his team have shown in recent weeks, having recorded three wins in their last four games across all competitions.

Genclerbirligi secured a 1-0 home victory over Gaziantep in their last league game, having also recorded consecutive 5-0 victories over Alanyaspor in the league and Karakopru in the Turkish Cup, with the 3-0 away defeat to Besiktas being the only blemish in that run.

Samsunspor Turkish Super Lig form:.

Genclerbirligi Turkish Super Lig form:.

Genclerbirligi form (all competitions):.

Samsunspor will be without Celil Yuksel, who is recovering from a hamstring injury, while Fatih Kaya and Yunus Emre Cift are also unavailable.

Emre Kilinc is a doubt, leaving Bjelica with a few selection decisions to make, although Mohamed Bayo is expected to lead the line again after scoring his first goal of the season against Galatasaray.

Genclerbirligi have several absentees, with Dimitrios Goutas ruled out for the season due to a cruciate ligament injury.

Kevin Rodrigues is also dealing with an injury, while Peter Etebo, Gokhan Akkan and Ensar Cavusoglu are doubts.

Samsunspor possible starting lineup:.

Bayazit; Mendes, Erakovic, Drapinski, Tomasson; Sekongo, Watt, Ohlenschlaeger; Coulibaly, Bayo, Sousa.

Genclerbirligi possible starting lineup:.

Egribayat; Tongya, Celik, Niasse, Aydar; Diabate; Traore, Ulgun, Luis, Gouveia; Mendes.

Samsunspor have been struggling badly in recent weeks, but their home victory over Konyaspor reveals they are still capable of producing a positive result in front of their supporters.

The visitors have enjoyed a better campaign overall and arrive with greater confidence after beating Gaziantep, but their away performances remain a major weakness.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thomas Frank believes his first win as Crystal Palace manager can be a “turning point” in the club’s season.
  • Palace sit bottom of the Premier League table but tasted victory for the first time in Frank’s tenure with a 2-1 win over 10-man Real Sociedad in his second game in charge.
  • The Eagles came from behind after trailing to a second-half goal by Chelsea loanee Mamadou Sarr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thomas Frank believes his first win as Crystal Palace manager can be a “turning point” in the club’s season.

Palace sit bottom of the Premier League table but tasted victory for the first time in Frank’s tenure with a 2-1 win over 10-man Real Sociedad in his second game in charge.

The Eagles came from behind after trailing to a second-half goal by Chelsea loanee Mamadou Sarr.

But Jean-Philippe Mateta levelled from the penalty spot after Jon Martin was shown a second yellow card and sent off for the side sat fifth in La Liga.

Palace then scored their eventual winner through substitute Dwight McNeil but almost threw it away when Dean Henderson was required to make a last-gasp save after Yeremy Pino had seen the Eagles’ second spot-kick of the night saved.

Palace’s victory came five days after their 3-2 defeat at Coventry in Frank’s first match in charge.

“In the second half I felt we kept the ball much better,” Frank noted after his side’s victory on Thursday.

“What I really liked was the belief from the players. It is so important to keep doing the right things and keep believing.”.

Palace were guilty of giving the ball away in poor errors and handing Sociedad some cheap chances despite eventually closing out a victory.

Frank mentioned: “We should just control that game. But we probably don’t have the confidence right now.

According to recent reports, asked whether the win against Sociedad can be a turning point in a so-far difficult season for the south Londoners, Frank replied: “I think it could be. But we need to follow it up, of course, with a good performance against Hull on Sunday. But there were a lot of positives from this game.”.

Your weekly briefing on Chelsea, featuring team news and expert analysis from Dom Smith.

In a recent development, I would like to be emailed about offers, event and updates from Evening Standard. Read our privacy notice.

Xabi Alonso says he takes the “whole responsibility” for Chelsea’s dismal defending but disagrees with his friend Jamie Carragher that Wesley Fofana and Levi Colwill will never be a good enough centre-back pairing for the Blues.

Fofana and Colwill were heavily criticised for their performances last Saturday as the west Londoners were thrashed 4-1 at home to Leeds in the Premier League.

The defeat exposed further weaknesses in Alonso’s defence and proved the worst possible response to their disappointing previous outing, the 1-0 defeat to Sunderland before the international break.

Chelsea head to the City Ground to face Nottingham Forest on Friday night eager to get back to winning ways.

Analysing the Leeds loss, Carragher noted on Sky Sports: “Chelsea have got a massive problem at centre-back and if they don’t change it in January, they’re going to have a big problem in terms of where they feel they should be this season with the Champions League.”.

Speaking about Fofana and Colwill, he added: “As a partnership, this will never work because they’re not physical enough and there’s no real leader there.”.

Industry observers note that asked whether he had seen these comments from his former Liverpool team-mate, Alonso mentioned he had not, before adding: “I must disagree. I disagree with Carra. For sure, you can have bad games. We were not good [against Leeds]. But I think I’ve seen them [Colwill and Fofana] play well, and I’ve seen them show good levels.

“This is the goal and the challenge – to be consistent in the performance and to be consistent in the basics and not to drop in certain games when we are facing a tough opponent.”.

It has been revealed that alonso, speaking more broadly about Chelsea’s poor defending, added: “There are no excuses not to do better. We are in the process. Taking steps, taking a step forward but until it is totally in the DNA of the team it takes time.

In a recent development, “I take the whole responsibility of the team and how they perform. We need to show [improvement against Forest], not just talk. Talk is cheap. It’s about performing on the pitch.

“We want to be back on that more solid feeling that we had. This was hopefully one-[off], and we don’t want to repeat it.”.

Latest Update: Engineering signalling centres to trigger human trunk morphogenesis in vitro

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 37 min read (7378 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~37 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that vertebrate trunk development is orchestrated by endogenous signalling centres that generate gradients of signals such as WNT and BMP to pattern cell fates and drive morphogenesis1,2,3,4,5,6,7.
  • This is a preview of subscription content, access via your institution.
  • Access Nature and 54 other Nature Portfolio journals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that vertebrate trunk development is orchestrated by endogenous signalling centres that generate gradients of signals such as WNT and BMP to pattern cell fates and drive morphogenesis1,2,3,4,5,6,7. Whether these cues alone can reconstitute human trunk-like morphogenesis in vitro remains unknown. Here we present a synthetic embryology platform for high-throughput, spatiotemporal delivery of morphogen signals to epithelial cysts derived from human pluripotent stem cells. Transient WNT and BMP gradients are sufficient to drive the generation of axially elongating trunk-like structures that contain a central neural tube flanked by axial, paraxial, intermediate and lateral mesoderm. The geometry of the transient BMP signal exerts lasting control over mediolateral patterning and bilateral symmetry. Patterning and morphogenesis are sustained by neuromesodermal and lateral plate mesoderm progenitors induced by the initial cues, which act as endogenous signalling centres. Together, these findings define a minimal spatial code sufficient to reconstitute trunk-like morphogenesis in a human stem-cell-based model and establish a scalable platform for studying early human development and congenital disorders.

Sources indicate that the scRNA-seq and bulk RNA-seq data generated for this study are available from the GEO under accessions GSE306808 and GSE347564, respectively. Sequencing reads were aligned to the GRCh38 human reference genome (10x Genomics GRCh38-2020 for scRNA-seq; Ensembl GRCh38, assembly accession GCA_000001405.29, for bulk RNA-seq). Previously published29 human embryo scRNA-seq data are available from the GEO under accession GSE155121. Other reanalysed datasets are available from the following repositories: mouse gastrulation, ArrayExpress (E-MTAB-6967)55; cynomolgus macaque embryo, GEO (GSE193007)56; RA-gastruloid, GEO (GSE208369)57; axial organoid, GEO (GSE220563)17; axioloid, GEO (GSE199576)18; and segmentoid, GEO (GSE195467)19. GEO series are accessible at https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/ and ArrayExpress experiments at https://www.ebi.ac.uk/biostudies/arrayexpress. The confocal and time-lapse datasets are large multichannel image series that are impractical to deposit in full; the measurement tables from which the quantitative imaging panels are plotted are provided in the code repository (Code availability). Raw imaging data, and any additional information required to reanalyse the data reported in this study, are available from the lead contact, S.R., on request; requests will be answered within 1 month and data shared by secure electronic file transfer without restriction. Source data are provided with this paper.

Custom code for image analysis and for bulk RNA-seq and scRNA-seq analysis—including SMD feature selection, clustering and annotation, and the trunk morph–embryo correspondence analyses—is available under the MIT License at GitHub (https://github.com/stevenzwick/zwick-2026-trunk-morphogenesis) and archived at Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22756590)58. Random seeds and exact parameters (intensity thresholds and gates, background offsets, local-threshold window sizes, Gaussian σ, histogram edges, clustering resolutions and curated gene lists) are provided in the repository.

Recent findings suggest that a, A detailed schematic of the workflow is shown: (i) Matrigel is microcontact printed onto the two-layered PDMS stamp (PDMS-ii) using a flat PDMS stamp (PDMS-i). (ii) A thin PDMS microwell array is peeled from the silicon master and overlaid on a glass coverslip. Taller PDMS sidewalls are plasma-bonded along two edges. (iii) Capillary water flow through the microchannels drives localized Matrigel transfer from stamp PDMS-ii onto the PDMS microwell layer at the contact interface. (iv) Cells are seeded onto the transferred Matrigel pattern, overlaid with a silanized coverslip atop the sidewalls, and cultured further with media and microwell-trapped beads. b, Photographs of the experimental setup corresponding to steps a(i–iii): coating the flat stamp (grey border, fourth column, top); PDMS-ii stamps with different patterns (blue border, first column); PDMS microwell layer with wells at different positions (red border, second column); aligned PDMS-ii stamp and PDMS microwell layer in contact (green border, third column); and the application of weight and water flow for transfer (green border, fourth column, bottom). MG, Matrigel; RT, room temperature.

a–d, Design of two-layer PDMS stamp and microwell substrate: a, upper-layer pattern used to print Matrigel features; b, lower-layer embedded microchannels (white denotes channel features); c, assembled two-layer PDMS stamp with a three-dimensional illustration of the assembled stamp below; d, alignment of stamp features and microwell layer, with 120 µm diameter microwells positioned at defined distances from pattern edges. Scale bars, 1 mm. e, Whole-chip images show humidified microcontact printing (HµCP) of Matrigel mixed with fluorescently conjugated BSA (cyan) onto PDMS microwell chip (brightfield, grey), using a four-square stamp pattern. Air bubbles beneath PDMS microwell layer and above glass coverslip are visible in brightfield images. Images are representative of 6 independent experiments (12 chips) with similar results. Scale bars, 1 mm. f, Whole-chip image highlights standard microcontact printing (µCP) of fluorescent BSA onto glass to validate stamp pattern from a. Image is representative of 2 independent experiments (5 chips) with similar results. Scale bar, 1 mm. g, Image shows pluripotent epithelial cysts formed 3 days after seeding on a PDMS microwell chip, using stamp pattern from a. A diversity of cyst arrangements, rather than the optimized hexagonal pattern with a central cyst as in Fig. 1, are used to show the flexibility of the approach. Image is representative of 79 independent experiments (145 chips) with similar results. Scale bar, 1 mm. h, Whole-chip epifluorescence image shows pluripotent cysts (DAPI, grey), well-trapped BMP4-coated beads (pseudocoloured red), and pSMAD1/5/9 immunofluorescence (pSMAD, green) 6 h after bead deposition. Image is representative of 6 independent experiments (13 chips) with similar results. Scale bar, 1 mm. i, Representative higher magnification images of cyst arrays with adjacent BMP beads and pSMAD1/5/9 immunofluorescence 6 h after bead deposition, from three independent experiments. (Top row) Five-cyst arrays with one or two beads, from chip in h. (Bottom left) Seven-cyst array with two beads, from an independent experiment. (Bottom right) Five-cyst array with three beads, from an independent experiment. Scale bars, 100 µm. j, (Left) Plot shows normalized pSMAD1/5/9 intensity (pSMAD/DAPI) versus distance from BMP bead, d, for all cysts from chip in h except cysts at centre of arrays (n = 201 cysts; light grey lines, individual cyst profiles; solid lines, mean; shaded areas, ±1 s.d.). (Right) pSMAD1/5/9 intensity in the bead-proximal epithelium of each cyst is plotted against the distance to the nearest bead, dmin, showing a negative correlation (red line, R2 = 0.624; n = 156 cysts) up to a distance of 635 µm, beyond which the intensity is low and uncorrelated (R2 = 0.061; n = 45 cysts). k, (Left) Normalized pSMAD1/5/9 is plotted against angle relative to bead direction (θ - θb) for cysts within responsive regime (d < 635 µm; n = 156 cysts). (Right) The direction of the pSMAD1/5/9 distribution, quantified by its first moment, is plotted as a function of the angle towards the nearest bead, θb (R2 = 0.17, n = 156 cysts). The correlation between pSMAD1/5/9 direction and bead angle is weaker than in Fig. 1f due to the overlapping influence of multiple BMP beads positioned near most cyst arrays in h.

Cysts are from another chip of the same design (Extended Data Fig. 2a). Images are representative of 3 independent experiments with similar results. g, Pixel-density plots of FOXA2 versus FOXF1 (top) and SOX2 versus FOXF1 (bottom) immunofluorescence in day 2 cysts, indicating mutual exclusivity. Colour, log-scaled pixel density normalized to the 99th percentile of bin density; contours, equally spaced iso-density lines; dashed lines, positivity thresholds; percentages, fraction of pixels in each quadrant. n = 7 biologically independent cysts from 3 independent experiments. h, Images of cysts after 2 days of differentiation show FOXF1+ nascent LPM located proximally to BMP beads, FOXA2+ anterior mesoderm distant from beads, and TBXT+ mesoderm at posterior end of cysts. Two-sided Welch’s t-test: t = −7.00, d.f. = 2.5, P = 0.010, mean difference −28.1 CPM (95% CI, −42.3 to −13.9). *P < 0.05. k, Quantification of pSMAD1/5/9 in cells at the edge following 30 min treatment with 10 ng ml−1 BMP4.
