Derek McInnes last night hit out at his dozy Rangers side for switching off in the latter stages of a hard-fought 3-2 home win over Aberdeen and warned them they will be made to pay over the course of the season if they carry on being so naive.

Goals from Ryan Naderi, Djeidi Gassama and Raskin in the first ten minutes of the second half put the Ibrox outfit in total command after Brad Lyons had put the visitors a goal up at the break.

However, Findlay Marshall made it a nervy finish for Rangers after scoring for the Dons on 58 minutes and it took a brilliant save from keeper Ivor Pandur to deny Nicky Devlin before Rangers saw it out to take their unbeaten run to 14 games and close the gap on Celtic at the head of the Premiership to just one point.

It has been revealed that ‘I am relieved to win,’ mentioned manager McInnes, who made three changes and altered the shape at the interval. ‘I thought we only played with the intelligence, speed and intensity for about 20 minutes and, in that period, showed how good we can be.

Recent findings suggest that ‘But we put the game at risk. We lost a cheap goal and weren’t aggressive enough. We lost two goals, really, from set-plays.

‘At 3-1 up against a team as game as Aberdeen were — and they were really good value — our naivety for the second goal is beyond me.

Rangers boss Derek McInnes was relieved to win but urges his side to keep focused.

Nicolas Raskin slots home the third goal for Rangers in their thrilling 3-2 win over Aberdeen.

Recent findings suggest that ‘I am not sure it was a free-kick in the first place, but we turn our backs. It is almost as if we are in a daydream and we allow them to manipulate the ball. Great finish from wee Findlay Marshall, but we put ourselves in the mire there by just knocking off.

Industry observers note that ‘We were so naive at times in the game. We scored good goals at good times but I still think Aberdeen will be disappointed not to get something.

Sources indicate that ‘We should have stayed in charge of the game and the second goal we lose allows Aberdeen to keep going with a bit of oxygen and carry a threat. I am disappointed with the lack of control in the game and I am not really happy with a lot of what we saw.

‘That has to change because we will not always be able to outscore the opposition.

‘We hit Aberdeen like a train in the second half and they found themselves 3-1 down because of the quality and intelligence of our play. For whatever reason, we then started playing back the way again. We played more passbacks to my goalkeeper than I can remember in a long time.

In a recent development, ‘We need to play forward and show more control in the game. I am looking for better from my team.’.

Raskin, meanwhile, has urged his Rangers team-mates to blast themselves to the top of the table on Saturday night and really pile the pressure on arch-rivals Celtic.

The Light Blues play host to third-placed Falkirk on Saturday afternoon with Celtic going to Hearts the following day and the Belgian midfielder wants to make sure they don’t let the defending champions off the hook the way they have in previous years.

Industry observers note that ‘We need to keep it going,’ said Raskin. ‘In recent years, we have not been able to put enough pressure on the other team and now we are doing it, so that is good.

‘We will see how everybody reacts after next Saturday.’.

Djeidi Gassama scored to complete a stunning turaround for Rangers early in the second half.

Raskin has also revealed it took a stern half-time team talk from manager McInnes along with those substitutions to spark his side into life after a dreadful first-half performance.

In a recent development, ‘I think we made the game hard for ourselves in the first half,’ mentioned the Belgian. ‘The manager had an honest discussion in the dressing room and we came back and scored two early goals, which helped. But we weren’t focused enough after the third goal and conceded to make it even harder.

In a recent development, ‘We indicated character again. The manager remarked what a manager has to say when you are losing, playing badly, you are 1-0 down and you have to win the game.’.

Aberdeen boss Mario Frick left Ibrox feeling his side had missed a real opportunity.

‘I am disappointed with the five or six minutes after half-time. That hurts,’ he said.

‘We saw a good performance, Rangers were beatable tonight.

Recent findings suggest that ‘We need more time. We have to improve. We have to talk about those ten minutes. After 3-1 down, we came back and we believed in ourselves. We deserved an equaliser.’.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Andrew M here after a couple of days ‘off’, but not the kind where you sit in a hammock and have delicious things brought to you. More the kind where you have three stab wounds in your abdomen and a chunk of your insides taken out. If at all possible, I seriously recommend the former to the latter. Anyway, I’m here right now with coffee and painkillers, which I guess is something akin to Arseblog heritage.

Sources indicate that the Interlull is over and that’s it now until March. It’s non-stop Arsenal all the way, and all the focus will be on us and what we can produce on the pitch. For those interested in what our players got up to during this break, and what they delivered for their respective nations, Andrew A has a handy round-up over on Arseblog News. Now it’s about keeping everyone as fit as possible, the manager using the squad in the smartest and most effective way he can, and for some of the players who are capable of producing more doing exactly that.

I was quite interested in Lewis’ quick look at Viktor Gyokeres and his key pass metrics from yesterday’s blog: He’s delivering a key pass every 28.4 minutes. Last season he had a key pass every 104 minutes across those two competitions [PL & CL].

Industry observers note that I think sample size might be a factor here, because when you look at his xG per 90, it’s 0.05 per 90 in both Premier League and Champions League this season, versus .99 and .76 per 90 last season, but obviously he played more minutes last time out. After 14 appearances this season, he’s rustled up a total of 614 minutes; this time last season his first 14 appearances brought him a cumulative 1200+ minutes. The absence of Kai Havertz was a factor, obviously, but it was probably that early season load that contributed to the injury he picked up against Burnley after a solid first half performance.

It has been revealed that the job for Mikel Arteta is to find a way to share those minutes effectively, to have both his strikers scoring and assisting, and to harness some of what Gyokeres has been able to produce for Sweden. It’s often mooted that as a team we need to play to his strengths more, but perhaps these key pass metrics show that the design is more about eliminating some of the weaknesses in his game to make him more effective in the final third for us. Let’s see how it goes.

In a recent development, meanwhile, the KMI (Key Match Incident) panel have ruled on the Kai Havertz penalty incident against Hull. They ruled 5-0 that the on-field decision was wrong and that VAR, manned that day by Michael Oliver, should have intervened:.

Industry observers note that although Havertz is clearly in an offside position, there is a clear and impactful holding action by Mendy before any potential offside offence by Havertz. Given the chronology of events, a penalty should have been awarded. The panel considered the VAR intervention was correct; however, the outcome after the on-field review was considered to be incorrect as a penalty should have been awarded.

In a recent development, I get every day is a learning day for ‘ProRef’, the people whose job it is to know the rules of football but week after week seem to demonstrate in new and inventive ways that they don’t. The question for us as fans is, what are we supposed to do with this? Are we supposed to feel better knowing that they’re owning up to mistakes? It feels a bit like getting run over when you have the green light at a pedestrian crossing, a nearby cop just lets the bloke go, but then later a judge says he should have been stopped and arrested.

In a recent development, which is all well and good when you’re in a hospital bed in traction with a couple of broken legs and smashed pelvis (I say this only because I remember being in hospital with a bloke who fell under a bus and that’s what happened to him. He was fine though, his mates brought him in loads of joints which he used to share in the smoking room – this was 90s hospital). Which is to say, the damage has been done, the admission the bloke got it wrong in the first place doesn’t really make you feel any better.

From our perspective at least, Martin Odegaard’s winner ensured that decision didn’t turn out to be one which went on to live in infamy – like not drawing the lines for that Brentford goal that time, but it’s still essentially useless. Not least because you just know this weekend or next weekend some other mad thing will happen and they’ll say ‘Oooops! Sorry about that LOL here’s Michael Owen and Howard Webb!’, and some team will lose points because they can’t properly apply the rules of the game to things that happen on the pitch.

Finally for today, we’re being linked with a January move for Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott. He’s certainly a fine player, but it doesn’t make a lot of sense to me given we already have the best midfield depth in the Premier League, and beyond. Where does he fit with Declan Rice, Bruno Guimaraes, Martin Zubimendi, Mikel Merino, Myles Lewis-Skelly and Martin Odegaard? Perhaps if, for example, Zubi went there’s a case to be made for a replacement, but as it is he’s struggling for minutes anyway, and you don’t pay that kind of money for someone to come in and be peripheral.

It has been revealed that like most of you, if there’s money to be spent in January, I’d much rather see it go on the forward line where I feel like there’s obvious room for improvement and to increase our depth. The left hand side is the obvious place, it’s hard not to worry about the right a little bit with Bukayo Saka’s injury, and the striker conversation is one which is never quite going to go away. So, on that basis, links to Scott don’t really add up for me. Unless Arteta fancies converting him to another left-back. Then it all clicks, but I think there’s one Bournemouth player we’d all rather see arrive.

Industry observers note that right, I’m gonna leave it there for this morning. In terms of a podcast, I’m not quite feeling up to it today, but what we’ll do is make our Patreon preview podcast free and available to everyone tomorrow afternoon. I should be less sore then, and I continue to be blown away by your many emails and messages. Thank you so much, they mean the world.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the course of the November international break, news of contract extensions for some of Arsenal’s ‘pillar’ players has begun to filter through. David Raya, Jurrien Timber, Declan Rice and Piero Hincapie are all reportedly on the verge of new deals, with Riccardo Calafiori’s deal also in the in-tray for Andrea Berta too.

Industry observers note that arsenal have assembled an elite core and it didn’t happen overnight. Back in the summer of 2021, the club enacted a policy of buying players under 24 years old. I always felt like this was the true year zero of the Arteta project. That always felt like the window that built the foundations.

In hindsight, it’s interesting that only Ben White and Martin Odegaard have ‘survived’ since then, with Ramsdale, Tomiyasu, Lokonga and Tavares all having drifted away ever since. Emile Smith Rowe also signed a upcoming contract and took the number 10 shirt that summer and now he is scratching around for minutes at Fulham.

It has been revealed that the summer of 2022 saw the arrivals of Gabriel Jesus and Alex Zinchenko, as well as Fabio Vieira. The former pair briefly elevated Arsenal to a newly introduced level before becoming quickly obsolete. Vieira was a fairly pricey gamble that didn’t pay off. It was the summer of 2023 that truly established Arsenal among England’s elite. David Raya, Jurrien Timber, Declan Rice and Kai Havertz’s arrivals turned Arsenal from caterpillars to butterflies.

Three of those players are about to sign upcoming contracts. Curiously, we have little to no reporting on whether Kai Havertz is lined up for a new deal as yet. Arsenal are banking on their well assembled core to deliver more silverware as they enter their peak years (Raya is 31 which feels close to peak age for a goalkeeper).

Recent findings suggest that undoubtedly, there are some players who will drift away in the coming years. Mikel Merino, Martin Zubimendi and Ben White feel unlikely to get upcoming Arsenal contracts at this particular moment in time. (Though these things can and do change). Like Havertz, Odegaard’s deal runs until the summer of 2028 and we have yet to hear rumblings of a new deal.

Recent findings suggest that odegaard and Havertz have negotiated significant fitness challenges over the last two seasons, which probably explains why they have found themselves lower down Berta’s to do list. Timber has had his own physical challenges too, but he is 25. Havertz and Odegaard are 27. Their next contracts will be their last ‘substantial’ contracts in terms of wages and their resale value will drop to close to zero if Arsenal tie them down. It makes sense for the club to take its time a little more with both players.

According to recent reports, both are also defining attacking and / or creative players in the Arsenal team. At some point, Arteta is going to have to plot an evolution within this core and it feels like that is more likely to happen in the final third of the pitch than within the core of players who operate behind the ball. Behind the ball, Arsenal are absolutely tip top and have some of the most elite players in the world in their positions.

That is not as true ahead of the ball. Odegaard and Havertz remain, for my money, elite, defining players for Arsenal. For the purposes of this piece; I am going to speculate that Odegaard is going to be offered a fresh contract given his status in the team and because his role is a little more holistic and he doesn’t solely operate in the final third.

Recent findings suggest that which leaves us with Havertz. I rate Havertz really highly and believe he is integral to Arsenal’s style, he has the technical quality to play one touch football and the physical quality to act as a release valve and hold the ball up. I can’t think of many forwards who offer both sides of the game to such an extent.

According to recent reports, there are several Arsenal attackers I would trade in before Havertz. However, the market doesn’t always bend to your will. Arsenal remain a self sustaining club and in the PSR / SCR era, player trading has never been more important or more voluminous. Keeping money swishing between the cost and revenue columns is a necessity in this environment.

Clearly, the number one impediment to Havertz getting a fresh deal is his fitness. He is still clearly preferred by the manager to Viktor Gyokeres. I have to say I am surprised (a little unpleasantly) at how swiftly the tide of opinion has turned against Havertz. The run he went on very recently that saw him score in the Champions League Final, score the goal that clinched the title against Burnley, a critical goal against Chelsea and the winning goal at Anfield seem to have just bought him absolutely no credit within the fan base, which I find a little surprising.

However, Arsenal need to boost their attacking prowess overall at some point very soon. Like I said, I would consider Havertz a superior player to all of Eze, Gyokeres, Tzolis and Madueke. The squad is well served for numbers in attack; it doesn’t have any gaps in that respect. It has a gap in elite quality.

Industry observers note that the key to boosting that might not be ‘who is the least effective player?’ it might be ‘who is the most saleable?’ Sometimes you do just have to cash in your chips on a player to evolve and move forwards. It doesn’t always have to be because the player is obsolete or not good enough. Arsenal have such numbers in midfield that there also isn’t really a route into the team there for Havertz either.

If someone offered £60-70m for Gyokeres or Eze, I would accept it and give Havertz a new contract the next day (assuming he does prove his fitness). But I think those scenarios are unlikely. I am not arguing that we have definitely reached the ‘we must sell Kai’ stage and I will reiterate that, at this moment in time, I consider him a very key player who should pretty much always start when fit.

It has been revealed that while he isn’t the most prolific finisher as a centre-forward, crucial goals this season against Chelsea and Liverpool demonstrate his worth. The conversation about moving on only becomes live on condition that the money is used to immediately buy an obviously elite attacker- preferably a centre-forward in that case since that is the gap a Havertz departure would leave.

Recent findings suggest that but I am certain it is a conversation Arteta and Andrea Berta are at the moment entertaining. Arteta will want to push the level of the team even further and, to fund what that is going to entail, potentially painful sales will have to be made somewhere. The vigour with which the club pursued the sale of Gabriel Martinelli this summer shows the manager has the stomach for that conversation too.

Hugo Ekitike has been side-lined due to injury since April now.

The Frenchman managed to tear one the ligaments in his ankle with his return date not yet set in stone.

But, at the start of the season, Andoni Iraola did mention that Liverpool hope the striker is ready to feature in their final two games of the Champions League league stage.

If he can manage to do this, the second half of the Reds' season will certainly look much more positive than the first.

However, if upon his return he isn't back to his usual self, there are some options that Liverpool can explore with a deal for a new striker now emerging.

Gustavo Varela could become Liverpool's next Hugo Ekitike.

Last summer, a lot of people were questioning whether Liverpool had overpaid for Ekitike or not.

In the end, a deal worth around £70 million was agreed for the Frenchman with other clubs such as Newcastle United also interested in signing him.

He's performed fairly well during the 2024-25 season but, during his time with Paris Saint-Germain, things didn't really go to plan.

A lot of people suggested that the striker was too young and too raw for England's top flight but, fortunately, he managed to prove them all wrong.

However, Ekitike's injury set his progress back a bit with some people even suggesting that a new striker should be brought in to plug the gap.

Lewis Koumas eventually took up that role but, that doesn't mean that the Reds' don't have a trick or two up their sleeve, especially if this latest upgrade from Football Insider is to be believed.

"Liverpool will not prioritise a move to sign Monza striker Gustavo Varela in January, sources have told Football Insider," they wrote.

"The 21-year-old has emerged as a target for the Reds, having struck 11 goals from his opening 11 games in Serie A so far this term.

"The Reds are "keeping tabs" on the Portuguese youngster, with several top Italian clubs also having their "eyes fixed on him" at the moment.

"However, sources say that Varela is viewed as more of a long-term option at Anfield, and the club are not likely to make a move for him this winter.

"Monza are relaxed over their frontman's future for now, but they know that further interest from top clubs is inevitable if he continues to perform.".

Gustavo Varela could be Liverpool's next Hugo Ekitike.

Before the 2025-26 season kicked off, Gustavo Varela was a relatively unknown striker.

The 21-year-old joined Serie A outfit Monza for around €2.5 million in the summer with the deal not expected to cause that much of a stir.

However, to the surprise of many, the Portuguese attacker is currently the Serie A's top scorer.

He has 11 goals to his name and, despite all of his efforts, Monza are still sitting inside the relegation zone.

Obviously, this could just be a purple patch of form which is why the attacker is more of a long-term target rather than a short-term option.

But, if Liverpool do sign him, he could follow a similar path to Ekitike and prove the doubters wrong.

An asking price worth around €40 million has been mooted for the striker but, it's at the moment unclear whether the Reds would spend that much on him, even if this form does continue.

  • Manchester United could look to bring in competition for number one goalkeeper Senne Lammens next year, according to former Red Devils captain Ashley Young.
  • Lammens has made a series of mistakes in recent matches and has only managed to keep one clean sheet for the Red Devils this season.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Matt Law | 26 Nov 2026 19:37, Last updated: 26 Nov 2026 19:39.

Manchester United could look to bring in competition for number one goalkeeper Senne Lammens next year, according to former Red Devils captain Ashley Young.

Lammens has made a series of mistakes in recent matches and has only managed to keep one clean sheet for the Red Devils this season.

The Belgium international conceded a penalty against Sporting Lisbon in the Champions League on Wednesday evening and then dropped a clanger late on to allow Luis Suarez to make it 2-2 in Portugal.

Lammens also made a high-profile mistake for Belgium at the 2026 World Cup against Spain, and Young has said that the 24-year-old may be on the verge of being dropped.

Young has even suggested that Man United could look to bring in competition for Lammens next year if his struggles continue.

Senne Lammens with a gift for Luis Suárez to equalise for Sporting ? ? Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/kOQ6HImlVc.

"You look at the World Cup and the mistake he made, it's effected him massively. You just see it's mistake after mistake after mistake. He could be one mistake away from being dropped," Young told BBC Sport. "You've got Karl Darlow and Tom Heaton that are not really going to push Senne Lammens for that No.1 jersey, I do think Mauricio Pochettino is going to look and think 'If I can one of the keepers out of the door, and get someone in January to be pushing Lammens, then I will be doing that'. There's far too many mistakes.".

Man United head coach Mauricio Pochettino refused to criticise Lammens after the clash with Sporting despite the goalkeeper's unconvincing performance.

In a recent development, "This type of thing happens. That is football. Football is about making mistakes," Pochettino told reporters when asked about Lammens.

"I always want to support my player. I think we need to talk about responsibility. In this type of action our defensive line needs to cover the keeper better because it was very difficult.

"It's not to blame the defensive line, but it's two things that we need to improve - details that we need to work on. We need to manage his type of situation better.".

Lammens arrived at Man United from Club Brugge in the summer of 2025, and he has represented the Red Devils on 49 occasions, conceding 74 goals and keeping just nine clean sheets.

The Belgian is expected to keep his spot between the sticks for Man United's Premier League clash with Brentford on Saturday afternoon.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mikel Arteta’s press conference takes place early this morning, rather than the typical 1.30pm start time.
  • Recent findings suggest that so, the talking points will come later, if there are any talking points.
  • Recent findings suggest that also, the bloke from Sky Sports will come to the press conference dressed up as a PS5 controller to ask if the manager is concerned about his players staying up all night to to play Grand Theft Auto 6.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mikel Arteta’s press conference takes place early this morning, rather than the typical 1.30pm start time. I woke up a bit later than usual, and there’s part of me that wonders if I should wait for it before doing the blog, but then that would make the blog a lot later than usual and I don’t want to disrupt anybody’s routine. Especially on a Friday.

Recent findings suggest that so, the talking points will come later, if there are any talking points. My guesses on questions today:.

Recent findings suggest that also, the bloke from Sky Sports will come to the press conference dressed up as a PS5 controller to ask if the manager is concerned about his players staying up all night to to play Grand Theft Auto 6. Hopefully he requires a firmware update before speaking.

So, in the absence of news and stuff to talk about, I thought I’d point you in the direction of some stuff elsewhere. In a week where we’ve been handing out new contracts all over the place, Phil Costa wonders about the future of Kai Havertz and whether new terms might be on offer for him.

In a recent development, it’s an interesting one because I think it’s clear he’s the manager’s first preference from the two strikers he has available to him. If he was forced to drive deep into the woods and leave one tied to a tree, it’d be Viktor Gyokeres left in the dark forest to try and undo his knots and make his way back to civilisation. But reservations about Kai’s fitness are more than understandable, and while this is a player who has scored big goals for this club since his arrival, there are inconsistencies to his game that can be frustrating.

He turns 28 in June, which is far from over the hill, but it’s then about the cost of a multi-year commitment to a player who, more than likely, you’re probably never going to get much of a return on. Particularly if you have to add to what is already a significant weekly wage packet, even if others will have taken over the mantle of Arsenal’s best-paid player.

My gut feeling is that we’ll probably keep him though, and jokes aside it probably is connected to Gyokeres. The Swedish international feels like the player most expendable of the two in the manager’s mind, and I just can’t really see any scenario when simply Arsenal hang onto both for another season or two, or decide that both can be sold and then replaced at the same time. We sold two left-wingers and a striker this summer and replaced them with one single player, so it’s not as if our track record of augmenting the squad in forward areas would give you much confidence in our ability to undergo sweeping reform.

Thus, some consistency will be necessary, and if push comes to shove, Arteta will sell Gyokeres a hundred times before Havertz once – unless there’s something to do with fitness/injury. The question then is do we renew now, or see where we are next summer? If we add a younger striker to the mix, the benefit of Havertz’s experience isn’t to be underestimated, and then in those final 12 months, if there’s a deal to be done it can be done, and if not, the club have time to consider other options. At that point, he’ll be almost 29, he’ll have options elsewhere if there’s no future at Arsenal.

Of course players want some security when it comes to their contracts and their futures, it might be a case he wants that and that may force the issue one way or the other, but as it stands, it doesn’t seem to be an issue that absolutely has to be a top priority right now (unlike someone like Declan Rice, for example).

In a recent development, for more good reading this morning, Lewis writes about Thomas Frank and Mauricio Pochettino (the substantial lumpy prick), and the challenges they face with their newly introduced clubs. I know I said this on the Arsecast Extra earlier in the week, but I really feel like the latter escapes the scrutiny he deserves for the evil he has perpetrated throughout his career. Manager of Sp*rs, Chelsea and PSG, and now Man Utd, as well as a stint as a national manager during which I thought he thoroughly shamed himself over the Folarin Balogun incident in the World Cup. I know he’s a big mate of Mikel Arteta, but for me he’s up there with the worst of them. A Maroon5 cover of a Phil Collins song brought to life.

Right, I’ll leave it there. As I said yesterday, we’ll have a preview podcast over on Patreon later on, but in the absence of an Arsecast this week we’ll make it available to everyone for free via the usual podcast channels. That should be out after lunch at some time.

Newcastle a challenge but a good post-Interlull opportunity

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that arsenal are back in Premier League action after the Interlull with a trip to face Newcastle away from home.
  • In terms of the Arsenal team today, Arteta can flip a coin between Ben White and Jurrien Timber, both of whom were on the scoresheet for their countries during the break.
  • Industry observers note that in midfield there’s no Martin Zubimendi whose unfortunate run of injuries continues with a hamstring strain picked up playing for Spain against England.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that arsenal are back in Premier League action after the Interlull with a trip to face Newcastle away from home. It’s been a difficult place to visit over the years, and we’ve had some unenjoyable encounters – there particularly during Eddie Howe’s tenure. However, Mikel Arteta more or less has a full squad to choose from, and this version of Newcastle under latest manager Matthias Jaissle haven’t been at all convincing so far this season.

In terms of the Arsenal team today, Arteta can flip a coin between Ben White and Jurrien Timber, both of whom were on the scoresheet for their countries during the break. My gut feeling is that the Dutchman will start today with White penciled in for Borussia Dortmund in midweek. William Saliba is back after another behind closed doors appearance to build his fitness, but for a game that’s likely to be intense and physical, I can’t see anything other than Ezri Konsa alongside Gabriel today. The Frenchman often needs a game or two to get his rhythm back, and while friendlies are useful, they’re not quite the same as competitive minutes. He too is likely to feature in the Champions League on Tuesday.

Industry observers note that in midfield there’s no Martin Zubimendi whose unfortunate run of injuries continues with a hamstring strain picked up playing for Spain against England. The form of Declan Rice and Martin Odegaard means they’re first picks, and then it’s about how the manager views Bruno Guimaraes for a game like this. Even if Newcastle haven’t been great, the pantomime villain in midfield adds a layer of spice that is inevitable after his summer move. If he wants to keep the crowd quiet, he could choose Myles Lewis-Skelly, but he paid £75m for this player for a good reason, and I think we’ll see the Brazilian from the start.

He was a hugely key player for Newcastle, and while I don’t think his departure was among the most contentious we’ve ever seen, he will be a target for their fans, and perhaps for players who know him – and his temper – very well. You’d hope at 28 he’s mature enough to deal with all that, and I’m sure conversations will have been had about not rising to any bait. Arteta has said more than once recently he wants more from this player, where better to give that than his former club?

As for the front three, I think it will be Christos Tzolis and Noni Madueke either side of Kai Havertz. The injury news for Bukayo Saka means he’s going to miss another month, at least, so there’s a substantial onus on Madueke to continue his recent improved form, but we’ll need him to add end product to the one goal and one assist he’s provided in the league so far. Similarly, Tzolis had a bright-ish start to his Arsenal career, and while the hamstring injury was ill-timed, we need a player who is ostensibly our first choice left winger to start delivering more in terms of assists but especially goals.

Havertz got the winner away to Liverpool, but had frustrating moments at home to Hull. He’s got Viktor Gyokeres on the bench to put some pressure on him, but this front three has some convincing to do and today would be a very good day to produce performances and end product.

Arteta was asked if the atmosphere at St James’ Park isn’t quite what it used to be, because of the way the team has changed and the inconsistent form they’ve suffered so far this campaign. His message was clear:.

If that’s the case, it will be even more difficult, because they will be even better prepared, they will have even more necessity to do that, and that’s what we expect. We always expect the best version from the opponent. That’s how we have to prepare for the game, and that’s how we’re going to approach it.

So, there’s no chance he’s letting his team think for a second this might be easier because it’s not the same Newcastle that have caused us problems in recent seasons. Nevertheless, he must have looked at this team and some of the issues they’ve had under their newly introduced manager and recognised that this is an opportunity to go there with a settled side of his own in good form and come away with all three points.

It is always a challenge there, but this is a mature Arsenal that should be capable of dealing with a team that has just three wins from thirteen games in all competitions this season. You never take anything for granted, but if we can keep the ball in the early stages, get control, and perhaps even an early goal, the ingredients are there for us to make this a winning start to what is a tricky run of games over the coming weeks. Fingers crossed.

Right, I’ll leave it there for this morning. As ever, we’ll bring you live blog coverage of the game later, as well all the post-game stuff on Arseblog News like the match report, player ratings, manager reaction, quotes round-up and more. There’s also a preview podcast on Patreon if you need something to listen to ahead of kick off. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Matt Law | 26 Nov 2026 19:51, Last updated: 26 Nov 2026 19:55.

Manchester United will continue their Premier League campaign against Brentford on Saturday afternoon, and Sports Mole's Football Editor Matt Law has discussed all of the latest talking points surrounding the 20-time English champions.

Man United conceded the most goals, 36, the most penalties, five, and the most red cards, five, of any Premier League team this season.

The Liverpool game was controversial as well, with the red card for Leny Yoro that has since been rescinded. Isak does not have even a little bit of control of the ball. He has ballooned it 10 metres in front of him, and still, he is given the red card for that one.

In a recent development, that was a huge turning moment in the game. That is not to say that United should be going on and losing 4-0 at Anfield, even with 10 men, but it is a game-changing incident.

It leaves United on one Premier League win this season, down in 19th spot in the table, eight points from 11 games, which is absolutely horrendous. What I would say is it was a tough start for Pochettino. It was a massive game at Anfield against the Liverpool side that played well.

If you concede that red card and then the fact they score from the free kick, that is a real hammer blow, and then you have to hold on and try to keep it 1-0 going into the second half.

According to recent reports, united could not do that. The performance level was well off it again. They conceded four goals in each of their last two Premier League games. It is 23 goals conceded now in the Premier League in 11 games.

Recent findings suggest that this team just cannot keep clean sheets for love nor money, in the Premier League, in any competition. Not kept a clean sheet since the win over Sabah in the Champions League, their first Champions League game in the league phase.

Sources indicate that if you keep a clean sheet, you have got a really good chance of winning football games. If you concede two a game, three a game, you are just not going to pick up wins.

According to recent reports, the game against Sporting Lisbon was one we could do a two-hour podcast on. The first penalty against Sporting is very soft.

It has been revealed that if that is a penalty then we might as well pack up and do podcasts on something else, because I do not want to be a part of a game that says that is a penalty. The Senne Lammens one is a penalty. What is he doing? He is flying out.

Then the goal that was disallowed for Amad, how that is a foul from Tielemans I will never know. An absolute horrific decision. The Fernandes penalty is a penalty for me.

Recent findings suggest that I think it is a straightforward decision. I do not think it is a foul on Senne Lammens, and I also do not think it is a foul for the last goal.

Dorgu got penalised for jumping into the goalkeeper, but they are either both fouls or neither are fouls. The contact on Senne Lammens for the Sporting equaliser was soft. I do not think that should be disallowed.

I do not think the United goal should be disallowed. The late red card was clumsy from Tielemans. It is not vintage football, it is not vintage Man United. They struggled in the final third of the field. Zirkzee came into the side and did okay.

An interesting stat from that game was that United had 12 high turnovers against Sporting, their most in any game this season.

Sources indicate that it did feel like they were winning the ball back higher. They were definitely pressing more as a unit. The shape of the team was better. They need a centre forward. If they had had Sesko last night and that threat in behind, you feel like they could have picked up all three points.

They were decent on the ball, recovered well from going behind in the game. Sporting are a good side and have had good results in the Champions League this season.

They are a really strong team with really good players. There were positives from the Sporting Lisbon game, and it leaves them in a decent enough position in the Champions League.

According to recent reports, they need to beat Leipzig in the next European game if they are really going to push on. They have got Bayern Munich and Villarreal as well, and those are going to be difficult games.

From the Champions League point of view, I still think they are in a decent enough position to finish in, whether that is the automatic qualification places or ultimately the play-offs.

Sources indicate that dealing with the Premier League is where they need to focus. They have got three games in a row now before the Leipzig game: Brentford, Newcastle away, Coventry at home.

The next two home games are absolutely massive. If they get turned over here and then go to Newcastle and do not manage to get a win, and then Coventry pick something up against them, it is very difficult.

Sources indicate that I do not think United are getting relegated this season. I say that out of hope. I think they are going to be busy in January. They are going to have to be inventive.

Industry observers note that around £50m is the figure they are going to have to spend. They need to bring in three players: definitely a striker, definitely a centre-back, definitely a full-back.

Carlos Baleba is going to be back sooner than expected. They are going to hope to get Rashford back at some stage in the not-too-distant future. Those two did train in the gym ahead of the Sporting game. Shaw was back on the bench as well.

Pochettino mentioned he was proud of his players for their performance level in the Sporting game and for overcoming the adversity, because there were some really horrific decisions from the referee and VAR in that game.

According to recent reports, united have not had the rub of the green. With the Fernandes goal and the divot, they highlighted the earlier clip and it was Fernandes himself who had made that divot in the turf.

According to recent reports, he had had a heavy touch with his boot in the box, and they circled back and it was the one he had made. So he actually managed to assist himself with that bobble. There has been a lot that has gone against United this season.

According to recent reports, this is a really big game on Saturday afternoon and one I am hoping they can win against Brentford. First Premier League win for Pochettino. Go to the Newcastle game, can you get a point? Can you go there and beat Coventry? Can you beat Leipzig? Football changes very promptly. If you put three or four good results together, everyone feels different.

It goes in cycles. A big football match. Brentford, it is one of those games that back in the day, United at home to Brentford, you would think it is a gimme, a home win.

Sources indicate that but they are an excellent team, Brentford, sitting sixth in the table at the moment with 17 points. Going away from home brings its different challenges, and without Igor Thiago as well is a massive one.

I did also want to mention Senne Lammens' form, which is a concern for me.

Going back to the middle of September, Paul Scholes stated in a podcast, The Good, The Bad and the Football, that he questioned whether Lammens was good enough, at a stage when he was actually playing quite well.

Industry observers note that and I have to be honest, I am in that camp now. He is making a lot of mistakes.

There was one in the Sporting game last night where they did not concede from it, but he pushed the ball back into the middle and no one was on the rebound to put it away. The mistake for the second goal was a major one as well.

Recent findings suggest that his form is slightly concerning and his confidence looks shot at the moment. I think he starts here, but it will be interesting to see whether United ultimately think they might have to get another goalkeeper in at some stage.

RANGERS 3 ABERDEEN 2: Amid all the thrills and spills, McInnes' triple switch sparks second-half revival

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.
  • Published: 18:40 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 18:50 EST, 24 November 2026.
  • When these sides last met in the league at the end of August, Rangers were in such a dark place that you wondered if their season was already destined to be another thoroughly miserable episode.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.

Published: 18:40 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 18:50 EST, 24 November 2026.

When these sides last met in the league at the end of August, Rangers were in such a dark place that you wondered if their season was already destined to be another thoroughly miserable episode.

Coming just three days after going out of Europe — for the second time — to an ordinary Jablonec team, the slender win Derek McInnes’ side claimed at Pittodrie that day felt like a can being kicked down the road.

In a recent development, in those early weeks, the players looked lost. The manager admitted that he didn’t know what style of football he was watching. The supporters were preparing for a long, hard winter.

It’s remarkable what can come from one scruffy win on the road. From that point to this, McInnes’ men have now gone 14 games unbeaten in all competitions.

In a recent development, they have the League Cup final to look forward to next month. They are now just one point behind Celtic in the Premiership and look eminently capable of putting in a serious challenge for the title. In keeping with so many performances throughout this run, however, this wasn’t particularly convincing. Flat and rudderless for 45 minutes, Rangers were deservedly a goal behind at the interval.

Industry observers note that credit where it’s due, though. Their response at the outset of the second period was outstanding with three goals coming in 11 minutes courtesy of Ryan Naderi, Djeidi Gassama and Nico Raskin.

That ought to have been the platform for many more to follow. But the performance slipped back a level. Aberdeen scored once and could easily have scored again.

Raskin (right) and Gassama celebrate after combining to put Rangers 3-1 up.

Naderi capitalises on Muller's mishandling to fire Rangers level at the start of the second half.

It was a truly thrilling match, full of slip-ups, incidents and moments of brilliance. The final stages were a tough watch for the home fans who hoped against hope that they’d see their side ease towards a routine victory.

As at Fir Park on Saturday, though, Rangers found a way and added another win to the ledger. And provided that remains the case in the coming weeks and months, none of the light blue legions will be complaining.

Despite ultimately not having quite enough to take something, Aberdeen manager Mario Frick will have been encouraged by much of what he saw here.

Had it not been for that atrocious spell at the outset of the second period, he’d have fancied his men to take something.

Recent findings suggest that they certainly fashioned plenty of opportunities. It was the defensive side of the game which ultimately cost them.

McInnes drafted in Kevin Kelsy, James Penrice and Ben Godfrey with Dujon Sterling, Tuur Rommens and Kim Minsu dropping out. There was a change of shape too, with a switch to a 3-5-2. For the longest time, it did not work.

Lyons gets his head to Marshall's corner to put Aberdeen in front in the first half.

While Frick kept faith with the diamond-shaped midfield which served him so well in Ayrshire, he made three changes. In came Ayoub Mouloua, Afeez Aremu and Findlay Marshall at the expense of Hicham Mahou, Ante Palaversa and Stuart Armstrong.

Recent findings suggest that before the game, there was a minute’s silence in memory of the late, great Ralph Brand. What a pity a couple of clowns in the visiting section were unable to keep their mouths shut for that long.

Rangers started brightly with Penrice’s delivery from the left causing chaos. Dan Neil had a stab at it, then Naderi. Aberdeen survived.

It has been revealed that once Frick’s side settled, Nicky Devlin’s cross was met by Marshall. His header was straight at Ivor Pandur.

Rangers’ general play was broken, their build-up more ponderous than patient. Gassama did manage to drop a shoulder and get a strike away but Aremu’s positioning ensured Marius Muller was untroubled.

Naderi was again Rangers’ most effective player, although the bar was set pretty low initially. The Czech’s lay-off invited Godfrey to let fly. His strike was well off target.

It has been revealed that while Gassama got into plenty of promising positions, his crossing continually let him down early on. On the other flank, Badredine Bouanani could not do right for doing wrong.

In a recent development, when the ball broke kindly to Naderi on the edge of the box, Ibrox expected the net to bulge. This time the man of the moment fired over. Rangers’ efforts in the first half were summed up by Naderi being tripped by Gavin Molloy on the edge of the box. Bouanani’s effort from the free-kick was woeful.

Sources indicate that aberdeen were aggressive and organised. And when the moment arose, they went forward in numbers.

McInnes shows his delight after his half-time changes helped turn the game around.

They edged in front on the half hour after Marshall won a corner which was a consequence of Frick’s men being prepared to back themselves.

Marshall curled the set-piece deep to the far post. Brad Lyons seemed to be invisible to those in light blue as he made a late run. Olwethu Makhanya belatedly reacted but it was too late.

Lyons got enough on his header to beat Pandur and force Raskin to make the block behind his keeper.

Recent findings suggest that the minute the scoreboard indicated that VAR were checking for a goal, you suspected the Belgian hadn’t done quite enough to keep it out. After a lengthy delay came confirmation of that fact.

Industry observers note that how would Rangers respond up until the break? Not terribly well. Lyons’ crude foul on Gassama gave Bouanani a chance to make amends with a set-piece. This one smashed into the wall. Seconds later, the winger fired well over the top when he ought to have done better.

It has been revealed that the Dons could easily have doubled their advantage. Jack Milne carried well and rattled the ball into Kevin Nisbet’s feet. The forward played a smart pass around the corner. Mouloua was only denied by a terrific save from Pandur.

There was still time for Mouloua to be thwarted by the outstretched leg of Makhanya as he moved to turn home a cut back.

Recent findings suggest that bluntly, it was no surprise that McInnes made three changes at the break. Off came Godfrey, Kelsy and Bouanani. On went Minsu, Rommens and Findlay Curtis. The impact was extraordinary.

Re-energised, within 45 seconds Rangers were level. Minsu’s speculative shot did come through heavy traffic. Still, Muller had to hold it. Credit to Naderi for anticipating the fumble. The instant it bounced towards him, he instinctively lashed it home for his 10th of the season. Subdued to that point, the home fans roared their approval. And they’d swiftly be off their seats again.

As Aberdeen’s attack broke down, Naderi played a simple pass into space. Gassama had too much pace for the chasing pack. Did he have the finishing? Absolutely. What a turnaround.

Gassama squeezes his shot under Muller to put the home side ahead just after the restart.

In a recent development, two goals in 90 seconds then became three in 11 second-half minutes. Gassama did superbly to motor down the left, look up and play in Raskin. The Belgian smashed the ball back across goal and in.

Recent findings suggest that that should have been that. Yet three minutes later, the Dons were back within a goal of McInnes’ men. Afforded too much time on the left, Alexander Briedl picked out Marshall with his cross. Marshall swept it home with his left foot via the inside of the post.

Remarkably, the Dons might well have levelled. Pandur made a fine save when Minsu threatened to turn an Aberdeen corner into his own net. The ball bounced off Nisbet and just wide.

Terrific throughout, Marshall saw a good strike whistle just wide. The fact the Dons made Rangers sweat for the win will be some consolation.

The 2026 Globe Soccer Awards will be held on December 28 and AC Milan will be among the nominations.

The Globe Soccer Awards – nicknamed the ‘Dubai d’Or’ – are an annual event held in the United Arab Emirates, recognising players, coaches, clubs and industry executives. The upcoming 17th Edition is scheduled for 28 December.

Industry observers note that read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

According to recent reports, it was founded in 2010 by Tommaso Bendoni, Riccardo Silva (a Milan investor) and football agent Jorge Mendes. The ceremony is organised in partnership with the Dubai Sports Council and backed by bodies like UEFA, the European Club Association (ECA), and the UAE Pro League.

The AC Milan captain Mike Maignan is back to his best form with club and country, and he is one of ten candidates for the award of ‘Best Goalkeeper of the Year’.

The French goalkeeper will face Gianluigi Donnarumma, Thibaut Courtouis, David Raya, Diogo Costa, Joan Garcia, Gregor Kobel, Emiliano Martinez, Matvey Safonov and Unai Simon.

A post shared by Globe Soccer (@globesoccer).

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, Milan as a club have been nominated for the Fans’ Historic Club Award. The other nominees are Real Madrid, Al Ahly, Barcelona, ​​Celtic, Inter, Juventus, Bayern Munich, Liverpool, Manchester United, Benfica, Boca Juniors, River Plate, Penarol and Flamengo.

Fans will be able to vote until November 30th for 12 of the 14 categories, while in the second phase the public votes will be combined with those of the jury. You can cast your votes for Milan and Magic Mike here.

Newcastle 2-2 Arsenal: Two points dropped in a game of two halves

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1394 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Arseblog

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that in the cold light of day, it’s hard not to look at what happened in the 45th minute of this game as a key moment.
  • A good move down the left hand side saw Martin Odegaard square perfectly for Noni Madueke who arrived with pace, ready to finish first time.
  • It has been revealed that the lead had come via Eberechi Eze, finishing emphatically after superb work from Kai Havertz to rob the ball and play a deft pass behind the right back.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in the cold light of day, it’s hard not to look at what happened in the 45th minute of this game as a key moment. Arsenal were 1-0 up, well on top and absolutely deserving of the lead. Newcastle had struggled to exert any kind of control, and we’d already had 9 attempts on goal.

A good move down the left hand side saw Martin Odegaard square perfectly for Noni Madueke who arrived with pace, ready to finish first time. Unfortunately for him and for us, Lewis Hall produced a quite outstanding piece of defending to slide in and block the shot over the bar. That was the difference between Arsenal going in 2-0 up at the break rather than with just the single goal margin.

It has been revealed that the lead had come via Eberechi Eze, finishing emphatically after superb work from Kai Havertz to rob the ball and play a deft pass behind the right back. Newcastle’s only chance had come early, a shot from Jacob Murphy that deflected off his own player and drifted wide with David Raya wrong-footed. After that, we bossed the half, with 11 shots in total, 65% possession, but still only that one goal.

It feels redundant to say this is a very, very good Arsenal team, but if we have a weakness, it’s that we don’t turn this kind of domination into more goals. Very often we don’t need to as our defensive solidity and consistency keeps the opposition at bay, but last night we let our standards slip in that regard, and the lack of firepower or being clinical in the final third came home to roost.

It was, very literally, a game of two halves. Newcastle made a triple sub at the break and it would be churlish not to give them credit for the fact it made a positive impact. However, the Arsenal performance was night and day. The opposition upped the energy and intensity, and we made mistakes. Odegaard miskicking a Riccardo Calafiori throw-in provided them the opportunity to equalise, and I do wonder why Harvey Barnes was so free at the back post to slide home for 1-1.

It has been revealed that that goal gave them momentum, they caused us problems again and again, some of them of our own making with carelessness and misfortune. Eze got back well to defend in our box but unfortunately slipped, Raya’s clearance was unconvincing and then Gabriel had to boot the ball behind for a corner – from which they made it 2-1. Dan Burn drifted off Jurrien Timber to get a free header, the ball scrambled around a bit before Malick Thiaw poked it over the line to give them the lead. Messy, shambolic defending – not very Arsenal at all.

Sources indicate that if we’re being fair, we have to say they could have scored again. David Raya went off with a shoulder injury, Kepa had to make a smart save at the feet of Lewis Miley but why was he one on one with the keeper in the first place? A Joe Willock shot deflected wide in similar fashion to the Murphy one in the first half, and eventually Arteta changed things with Christos Tzolis and Myles Lewis-Skelly coming on for Eze and Bruno Guimaraes who had a quiet return to his former club – bar that first half moment when he almost got enough contact on a fantastic Declan Rice cross but could only put the ball wide from close range.

We did get an equaliser, and very well worked it was too. We played the ball across the back line from right to left, into midfield where Havertz’s smart dummy allowed Odegaard room to drive on and find Madueke. He was Arsenal’s best attacking player last night, he kept trying to make things happen, and while I think the Newcastle keeper will probably have nightmares about letting that shot in, Madueke deserved the goal, and it earned us a point.

It was after the 90th minute when the manager brought on Viktor Gyokeres and Mikel Merino to try and find a winner, the Swede had one shot over the bar from the edge of the box, but had we found another, it would have been a real smash and grab. In the end, the draw was probably a fair result based on how the game played out, and afterwards the manager was unhappy at leaving two points behind:.

In a recent development, my feeling is that we have lost two points today. And I say we because we were exceptional in the first half, from the beginning to the end. It should have been two, three or four-nil up, clear. But it wasn’t.

It has been revealed that we started to lose duels, we started to lose second balls. We gave the ball away and have really poor circulation balls against their press and their waves. And when that happens, you give them belief.

It’s a pity because the margin should have been, again, much bigger for the level that we’ve shown.

Industry observers note that and this is the key for me. It should have been, but it wasn’t, and it too often isn’t. As I stated above, our defensive brilliance is fundamental to us winning so many games, but football is a game of variance. You can’t always control everything. On another night Odegaard just puts his foot through that throw in and that first Newcastle goal doesn’t happen. Eze and Raya deal better with that situation and we don’t concede a corner. We can focus on those individual things and say we could and should do better for sure, but you have to allow for some of that over the course of a season. You cannot be perfect for 90+ minutes 38 games in every league campaign.

Sources indicate that the ongoing issue for me is our firepower though. I thought generally the front three played pretty well last night, and it’s not as if we missed a glut of chances, but it’s about turning the level of dominance we had in that first half into more goals. This isn’t a one-time issue either. We scored two lovely goals last night but we should have had that game firmly in our grasp at half-time, but in this league a single goal margin is never a sure thing.

Industry observers note that the summer was a let-down in an attacking sense, there’s no getting away from that. If we had a forward line that was even close to our midfield and defence in terms of quality and depth, the Premier League would be a cakewalk. I know that’s a bit simplistic, but it’s also a fact. Regardless of what you think of the business, we let goals go to Turkey and Saudi Arabia, and replaced them with a player who has yet to score. Which isn’t to lay the blame at the feet of Tzolis, far from it, but with the squad planning/building that was undertaken.

For me, January becomes increasingly important because the improvement required is obvious, and for a sporting director whose track record looks quite hit and miss as it is, he needs a convincing window or the questions around the job he’s doing will become louder and louder, and for good reason.

The other big problem from yesterday was the injury to David Raya. It didn’t look good at all, and any absence for him would be a huge blow to the team. He’s been the best in the Premier League, and perhaps the best in Europe, for the last 18 months, and inevitably there’s a drop-off when any club is without their first choice keeper for any period of time. That’s another adjustment we’re probably going to have to make, and if it means we’re likely to be less secure and clean sheets are harder to come by, then that issue of scoring goals and being more potent comes into even sharper focus. Let’s keep fingers crossed it’s not as bad as it appears to be.

Right, I’ll leave it there for now. There’s plenty to unpick from this one, so I’ll leave you to it in the Arses. More here tomorrow, including an Arsecast Extra. Until then, have a great Sunday.

Unconventional resistivity reduction in NbP semimetal nanoribbons

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 26 min read (5255 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~26 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that modern and future electronics harbour a key challenge: as conventional metal wires shrink to nanoscale dimensions, their resistivity increases sharply1 owing to surface and grain-boundary scattering.
  • This is a preview of subscription content, access via your institution.
  • Access Nature and 54 other Nature Portfolio journals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that modern and future electronics harbour a key challenge: as conventional metal wires shrink to nanoscale dimensions, their resistivity increases sharply1 owing to surface and grain-boundary scattering. To circumvent this unwanted behaviour, here, we explore the fundamental limits of charge transport in topological semimetal niobium phosphide (NbP) nanoribbons down to approximately 6-nm widths, with industry-friendly top-down nanofabrication. The extracted NbP nanoribbon resistivity reaches 18 ± 4.1 μΩ cm at room temperature with an approximately 9-nm2 cross-sectional area, lower than that of conventional metals and semimetals with comparable size. The NbP nanoribbon resistivity decreases with decreasing width, unlike the classical behaviour of metals such as copper. This trend suggests a growing relative contribution of surface and edge states as the nanoribbon cross-section is reduced, despite a certain amount of disorder, including edge roughness. Our findings advance the understanding of size-dependent transport and scaling in this class of semimetals, offering a platform for nanoscale wires and interconnects in future nanoelectronics.

The electrically-conducting width of this device is ~12.5 nm. b, Magnified view of the nanocrystalline NbP layer and crystalline Nb seed, together with their corresponding Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), obtained from the boxed regions in panel a. c,d, Bright-field image (c) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) elemental map (d) of the same device, showing distinct material compositions. In total, three NbP (1.5 nm) nanoribbons were examined by cross-sectional STEM. Across these samples, we observe consistent structural and compositional characteristics, including similar NbP crystallinity and sidewall oxidation, which support the scaling behaviour reported in this work. Additional STEM characterization was not performed on thicker NbP nanoribbons, as the thinnest nanoribbons are most relevant to the main conclusions of this study.

a, HAADF image of the NbP (1.5 nm)/Nb (3.4 nm) nanoribbon with an electrically-conducting width of ~18 nm. b, Magnified view of the nanocrystalline NbP layer and crystalline Nb seed layer, together with their corresponding FFT, obtained from the boxed regions. c,d, Bright-field image (c) and EDS elemental map (d) of the same device, showing distinct material compositions of each region. e, EELS linescan profiles of Nb (blue) and P (red) normalized intensity as a function of position along the direction indicated in panel c. f-h, Representative nanobeam electron diffraction (NBED) patterns extracted from 4D-STEM data at probe positions within the sapphire substrate (f), Nb layer (g), and NbP layer (h), with indexed reflections confirming the distinct crystal structure of each region. i-k, Orientation template matching of the representative NBED pattern in f–h, for the sapphire substrate (i), Nb layer (j) and NbP layer (k). Coloured symbols indicate the local crystallographic orientation of the best-matching template for that pattern. l-n, Phase template matching of the same patterns for the sapphire substrate (l), Nb layer (m) and NbP layer (n).

Sources indicate that a, Schematic of the scaling mechanism for conventional metals, with surface scattering and grain boundary scattering. b, As thickness and width of NbP are reduced, the conduction is consistent with the growing dominance of surface carriers, which are disorder-tolerant, with reduced scattering. The total sheet conductance in this case is a sum of the sheet conductance contributed from bulk carriers and surface carriers. c, For thick NbP, bulk carriers dominate the transport, and thus conventional scaling laws apply, with pronounced surface and grain boundary scattering. d, The Fuchs-Sondheimer (FS) and Mayadas-Shatzkes (MS) model fitting of 3.4 nm Nb seed layer, showing an excellent fit. The extracted resistivity with increasing width (W → ∞) is 56.3 μΩ∙cm, which matches the literature results. e, Sheet conductance (GNbP,□) of 1.5 nm NbP as a function of width (red curve), extracted from Fig. 2d of the main text. The sheet conductance from bulk carriers (extracted from Hall measurement) follows the conventional FS-MS scaling model (black dashed line), where the sheet conductance from surface carriers increases as the width decreases due to the increased surface area/volume ratio, as indicated by the purple dashed line. At this ultrathin thickness (1.5 nm), bulk carriers experience strong scattering, resulting in very small bulk carrier sheet conductance. f, GNbP,□ of 10 nm NbP as a function of width (blue curve). At NbP thickness of 10 nm, 3D bulk carriers and 2D top and bottom surface carriers contribute comparably to transport, as shown in Fig. 4b. At this thickness, as the nanoribbon width is reduced, the enhancement in surface conduction is insufficient to offset the increased scattering of bulk carriers. Consequently, bulk transport dominates in this regime, leading to a net reduction of sheet conductance (i.e., increased resistivity) with decreasing width, more similar to conventional metal wires. We note that there could be subtle differences in sidewall roughness and damage in the thicker nanoribbons compared to the thinner ones. See Supplementary Note 2 for the modelling details and more discussion.

In a recent development, a, Bulk Brillouin-zone schematic showing the two mirror planes and nodal rings from the band inversion. b, Representative band dispersion along Γ-S-M’, where the curves calculated without spin-orbit coupling (SOC) show the nodal-ring-related band inversion (plotted in green), and the curves calculated with SOC show the corresponding gap opening (black dashed lines). c, Real-space crystal view highlighting the helical states along the projected mirror line on the surface. d, Surface-state spectrum along \(\overline{\Gamma }\)-\(\overline{{\rm{X}}}\)-\(\overline{\Gamma }\)’, where the narrow Weyl-point window (grey shadow) hosts three pairs of helical states (indicated by arrows) that form the main part of the Fermi arcs, while remnant spin-split surface branches remain visible over a broader energy window (broad green shadow). Blue and red colours indicate the ‘± Sy’ spin polarization at opposite momenta, showing the helical feature. In summary, the narrow Fermi-arc structure is embedded inside a much broader nodal-ring-derived surface-state sector set by the band inversion. See Supplementary Note 7 for more discussion on bulk-topology hierarchy and topological surface-state interpretation.

a, Slab model along the [001] direction for the surface state calculations. Here, the 2 × 2 × 3 supercell is shown as an example. A 4.5 nm thick slab structure of the 1 × 1 × 4 supercell was used in the calculations. b,c, Surface band structures with Nb (b) and P (c) terminations along high-symmetry lines. Blue and red bands indicate the surface states of the Nb and P terminations, respectively. Bulk-projected states shown in pale blue are depicted as the background. The charge neutral point is set to 0 eV. d-f, Surface-projected Fermi surfaces with Nb (upper panels) and P (lower panels) terminations at 0 eV (d), −0.2 eV (e), and −0.4 eV (f). Darker colours represent larger contributions projected from the surface. Weyl points projected on the 2D Brillouin zone are shown as green and purple dots for opposite chirality. The constant energy cuts show surface-dominant open contours over a broad energy window, indicating that Weyl-derived surface bands persist even when the chemical potential is shifted deep into the hole-doped regime, which implies the robustness of the topological surface character. In addition, for the 4.5 nm thick NbP film, the top and bottom surface states exhibit minimal hybridization, except near the Weyl point projections where they meet each other. The Fermi-arc states remain largely unhybridized because they are well separated in momentum space. Even at momenta where they intersect, the resulting hybridization gap is negligible. See Supplementary Note 8 for the modelling details and more discussion.

It has been revealed that a, Slab model from the NbP (001) film with thickness d = 1.5 nm and width W = 4.4 to 5.7 nm. b, The one-dimensional (1D) band structure of a W = 5 nm nanoribbon along ky direction. The edge projection is highlighted in purple to show the edge states, while the bulk states are shown in pale blue. Near EF, the edge-projected subbands form an electron-like pocket, consistent with the negative pedge values (panel f). c-e, The spin projection to Sx (c), Sy (d), and Sz (e) components, respectively, for the edge state. The blue and red represent opposite signs of spin polarization. These edge states exhibit a pronounced spin texture arising from strong spin-orbit coupling (SOC) in noncentrosymmetric NbP where Sx and Sz components are locked to the ky momentum in a Rashba-type SOC. This reduces the wavefunction overlap between counter-propagating modes, thereby suppressing the leading backscattering channel, which indicates high-mobility edge conduction. f, The carrier densities from edge (pedge) and 2D film (p2D) are extracted from linear fitting of the total ribbon density (p1D) by p1D = pedge + p2DW, at varying W. Wc denotes the cross-over width at which the edge carrier density would dominate the transport over the top and bottom surface carrier density. Here, Wc ≈ 0 indicates that the enhanced edge conduction of ultrathin films is not primarily driven by an increased edge carrier density. Instead, it is more plausibly attributed to an enhanced carrier mobility arising from reduced backscattering as the edge dimension approaches the quasi-1D limit. See more details in Supplementary Notes 2 and 8. g, Agreement between the nanoribbon fitting (\({p}_{2{\rm{D}}}^{{\rm{NR}}}\)) and that obtained from independent slab film calculations (\({p}_{2{\rm{D}}}^{{\rm{slab}}}\)) which corresponds to the d = 1.5 nm thickness in Supplementary Fig. 10. This agreement supports the self-consistency of our calculations across both the nanoribbon and thin-film geometries.

a, Temperature-dependent effective resistivity (ρeff) of NbP films with different thicknesses up to 90 nm, measured from Hall bar devices. These films have a 3.4 nm Nb seed layer, whose resistivity is measured separately (black symbols). b, Low-temperature limit (2-10 K) of panel a. The smallest superconducting transition temperature Tc (~2.2 K) is in the 3.4 nm Nb layer (black symbols), while higher Tc are observed in the NbP/Nb films, and Tc decreases monotonically with thicker NbP. The symbol colours follow the convention in panel a. c,d, Temperature-dependent sheet conductance (GNbP,□) (c) and resistivity (ρNbP) (d) for all NbP thicknesses, after subtracting the Nb seed contribution. e, ρNbP as a function of NbP thickness at 300 K and 10 K. For comparison, the ρNbP values of nanoribbons with the widest widths (Fig. 2d of the main text) are slightly higher than those from Hall measurements at 300 K, possibly due to process-induced damage during nanofabrication. f, Temperature-dependent ρeff of a ~5 nm-thick Nb control film, measured from a Hall bar device. The residual resistivity ratio (RRR) is 1.48, and the Tc is ~4.2 K. Inset: enlarged view of the low-temperature region. The presence of NbP appears to promote superconductivity in NbP/Nb films. The superconducting proximity effect is one plausible interpretation, although changes in disorder and enhanced inter-grain coupling (in the presence of NbP layer) could also contribute. We also cannot fully rule out the formation of an interfacial superconducting layer at the NbP/Nb interface. The NbP sheet conductance is obtained by subtracting the sheet conductance of the Nb layer (measured independently on control Nb films) from the total sheet conductance of the NbP/Nb stack. The extracted NbP resistivity is then obtained by dividing the NbP thickness by the NbP sheet conductance, i.e. ρNbP = dNbP/GNbP,□, where GNbP,□ = Gtot,□ - GNb,□ and Gtot,□ = dtot/ρeff, where Gtot,□ is the total sheet conductance of the NbP/Nb stack, dtot is the total stack thickness and ρeff is the measured effective resistivity (panel a). The GNbP,□ (panel c) represents the NbP sheet conductance after subtracting the independently-measured Nb seed contribution. Additional validation of the subtraction method using Pt/Nb stacks is provided in Supplementary Fig. 19. Control experiments using Pt/Nb stacks validate that the subtraction procedure itself does not generate an anomalous resistivity trend. Nevertheless, the conductance of the Nb seed layer within NbP/Nb stacks cannot be independently measured and it cannot be noted, with absolute certainty, that its behaviour is identical to that of the separately measured Nb control film. Thus, the extracted NbP resistivity relies, by necessity, on the model used.

It has been revealed that a-c, Hall resistance (Rxy) vs. magnetic field (B) measured at various temperatures for 3.4 nm Nb (a), 1.5 nm NbP (b), and 10 nm NbP (c). For the NbP films (b,c), the Nb seed layer contribution is subtracted at each corresponding temperature to extract NbP Hall response, using the same two-layer Hall conduction model described in the supplement. d, Effective three-dimensional carrier density (p3D) for all films, revealing opposite temperature-dependence: ultrathin 1.5 nm NbP highlights an increasing p3D upon cooling, whereas both thicker NbP (10 nm) and Nb (3.4 nm) display decreasing p3D. (This figure is also included in the main text as Fig. 4d and is reproduced here for convenience). e, Effective hole mobility (μp) of the same films vs. temperature. NbP films exhibit a pronounced increase in mobility upon cooling due to suppressed phonon scattering, whereas the 3.4 nm Nb film shows only a slight rise in mobility, indicating that its transport remains strongly limited by surface scattering.

According to recent reports, a-c, Longitudinal sheet resistance (Rxx) vs. magnetic field (B) measured at various temperatures for films of Nb seed layer (3.4 nm) (a), for NbP (1.5 nm) on the Nb seed (b), and for NbP (10 nm) on the Nb seed (c). All measurements were performed with the magnetic field applied perpendicular to the film plane and current direction. At low temperatures, all films exhibit a pronounced negative cusp near low field regions, arising from the interplay of superconducting fluctuations and weak antilocalization. d-e, Longitudinal sheet resistance (Rxx) vs. magnetic field (B) measured at 1.8 K for both 1.5 nm thick NbP (on 3.4 nm Nb seed layer) and for the Nb layer (3.4 nm) evaluated separately. Measurements were performed with B field perpendicular to the film plane and current direction (d), and with B applied in-plane (e). The superconducting transition temperatures are Tc ~ 6 K for the 1.5 nm NbP (on Nb) and ~2.2 K for the 3.4 nm Nb film (see Fig. 3d of the main text). The upper critical field Hc2, defined as the midpoint between the normal state resistance and zero resistance, is extracted. At 1.8 K, the out-of-plane critical field \({H}_{c2}^{\perp }\) is 2.2 T for NbP (1.5 nm) and 0.38 T for Nb (3.4 nm). The in-plane critical field at 1.8 K exceeds 9 T for NbP (1.5 nm) and reaches 4.44 T for Nb (3.4 nm). The superconducting coherence length estimates are provided in the supplement. The sense current used for Hall bar measurements is 0.5 mA, corresponding to a current density of ~0.1 MA/cm2 for the NbP (1.5 nm) film and ~0.15 MA/cm2 for the 3.4 nm Nb control, with the same 100 μm Hall bar device width. We note that this sense current is well below the superconducting critical current: even when we increased the sense current up to 10 mA, we were unable to suppress the superconducting state at 1.8 K.

It has been revealed that a, Cross-sectional HAADF STEM image of the alternating NbP/Nb multilayers grown on sapphire. b-d, Denoised nanobeam electron diffraction (NBED) patterns extracted from 4D-STEM data for all Nb layers (Nb layers 1-3) showing consistent body-centred cubic (bcc) diffraction symmetry with indexed reflections, confirming crystalline quality across all Nb layers. Scale bars: 0.5 Å−1. e, EDS line scan across the multilayer stack showing Nb (blue), P (red), and Al (light brown) as a function of position, integrated over a ~ 5nm wide region along the direction indicated by the yellow arrow in panel a, confirming periodic composition and abrupt elemental transitions at each NbP/Nb interface. f-h, denoised NBED patterns from NbP layers 1–3, displaying diffraction symmetry consistent with the NbP crystal structure with indexed reflections, consistent with uniform phase and crystallographic orientation throughout the multilayer stack. The diffraction spots become progressively broader from layer 1 to layer 3, suggesting a gradual decrease in crystalline coherence in NbP layers further from the substrate. This is further supported by the emergence of diffuse ring features in the Layer 3 diffraction pattern, indicative of increasing structural disorder.
